story.title: Milo, Juno, and the Spark Brick
story.subtitle: A LEGO Adventure Across Time

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Spark Brick
chapters.text:
Milo built a tall LEGO tower on the rug. Juno stomped her toy dinosaur beside it. Rawr!

It was way past bedtime. Nobody cared.

Then one brick on the floor began to glow. Gold, then green, then gold again.

"Milo," Juno whispered. "That brick is awake."

Milo picked it up. It felt warm, like a tiny sun. It hummed a soft little tune.

WHOOOOSH! The room spun into swirly colors. The rug disappeared. Wood shavings covered the floor instead.

A man with a kind, tired smile was sawing a plank. Little wooden toys sat all around him.

"Welcome," he said. "I'm Ole Kirk. I'm a carpenter — that means I build things out of wood. I make toys here, in **Billund**, a little town in a country called **Denmark**."

"Since when?" Milo asked, brushing sawdust off his knee.

"Since **1932**," said Ole Kirk. "Wooden ducks. Wooden trucks. Even step-stools, so Mama can reach the top shelf."

Juno picked up a wobbly wooden duck. One wheel was crooked. She giggled and set it right.

"You fix things," said Ole Kirk, smiling wider. "I like that."

Milo looked around the busy little workshop. "Does your toy company have a name?"

Ole Kirk scratched his head. "Not yet, little carpenter. Not yet."

The glowing brick buzzed in Milo's pocket, like it was excited for what came next.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Name That Means Play Well
chapters.text:
Milo turned to Ole Kirk. "Does your toy company have a name yet?"

Ole Kirk grinned so wide his mustache wiggled. "It does, as of today."

"What is it?" Juno asked, hopping on one foot.

"LEGO," said Ole Kirk. "It's short for two Danish words — leg godt. That means play well."

Milo tried the words slowly. "Play... well."

"Just right," said Ole Kirk. He picked up a paintbrush and wrote big letters on his workshop door: **LEGO**.

The glowing brick in Milo's pocket buzzed and flashed gold, like it loved its new name.

"Here's something funny," said Ole Kirk. "Far away, in a very old language, the word lego also meant I put together. But that's just a funny accident. I picked the name for play well, not for that."

Juno giggled. "A name with a secret extra meaning!"

"PLAY WELL!" she shouted, stomping her dinosaur in a happy circle.

The workshop walls began to shimmer, like a pond when you drop in a stone.

"Hang on tight," said Ole Kirk, laughing. "Time to see what I build next."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Melting Machine
chapters.text:
CHUG. CHUG. CHUG-CHUG-CHUG!

A big noisy machine filled the new room. It smelled warm, like crayons left in the sun.

"What is THAT?" Milo asked, covering his ears.

"My newest helper," said Ole Kirk. "It's a machine that squishes melted plastic into any shape I want."

"Since when?" Milo asked.

"**1947**," said Ole Kirk. "I was one of the very first toy makers in Denmark to own one."

Juno peeked at a tray of little bricks popping out, warm and shiny.

"They have bumps on top," said Milo, "and holes underneath!"

"Those are called **Automatic Binding Bricks**," said Ole Kirk. "I made them starting in **1949**. Stack two, and they should hold together."

Milo stacked two. They wobbled. He gave the top one a gentle push. It slid right off.

"They don't really click," Milo said. "They just sit there."

Ole Kirk scratched his chin. "You're right. They need something more."

The glowing brick buzzed hard in Milo's hand, like it agreed completely.

"My son Godtfred has been thinking about that very problem," said Ole Kirk. "Want to meet him?"

"YES!" said Milo and Juno together.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Godtfred's Tubes
chapters.text:
A young man sat at a table, surrounded by wobbly brick after wobbly brick.

"Godtfred!" called Ole Kirk. "These two have an idea."

Godtfred looked up, tired but friendly. "I need one. These bricks keep falling apart."

Milo turned a brick over and peeked at the empty hollow underneath. "What if something was down here," he said, "to grab the bumps on the brick below?"

Godtfred's eyes lit up. He grabbed a pencil and sketched little round tubes inside the bottom of the brick.

"Tubes," he said slowly. "Like tiny hands, reaching down to hold on tight."

He rushed to the machine. CHUG-CHUG-CHUG! Out popped new bricks, each one hiding tubes underneath.

Juno grabbed two and pressed them together.

**CLICK!**

She pulled. They did not budge.

"IT CLICKS!" Milo and Juno yelled together.

"On **January 28th, 1958**," said Godtfred, "I'm getting a special paper for this brick design called a patent. It means it's really, truly ours."

Milo grinned. "Guess what? I have bricks just like this one, at home. A whole tower's worth."

Godtfred blinked. "Truly?"

"The very same tubes," said Milo. "Yours still fit mine, even after all this time."

Godtfred laughed, delighted. "Then I suppose we built something that lasts."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: LEGOLAND and the Giant Brick
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH! Sunshine. Flowers. Tiny brick houses as far as they could see.

"Where are we now?" Juno asked, shading her eyes.

"**Billund**, **1968**," said a cheerful voice. A guide in a straw hat waved them over. "Welcome to the very first **LEGOLAND**! It's a whole park built from LEGO bricks, right next to the old factory."

Milo spun in a circle, grinning at tiny brick giraffes and brick windmills.

Juno tugged his sleeve. "Look! A HUGE brick!"

She held up a brick as big as her hand.

"That's a **DUPLO** brick," said the guide. "Made in **1969**, just the right size for little fingers like yours."

Juno pressed it onto one of Milo's regular bricks. It held fast.

"It still fits!" she said, amazed.

"Big or small," said the guide, "every LEGO brick ever made clicks with every other one."

Juno set the giant brick on top of her dinosaur's back, like a saddle. The dinosaur toppled over sideways. Juno giggled so hard she snorted.

Milo laughed too. "Careful, you'll start a brick-saurus stampede."

The guide chuckled. "Ready for one more stop, you two?"

"ALWAYS!" said Milo and Juno.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Swap That Hat!
chapters.text:
The ground rumbled — tiny, friendly rumbles. Rows and rows of little LEGO people stood on a table, each one no taller than Milo's thumb.

"These are brand new," said the guide. "**1978**. We call them minifigures."

Milo picked one up gently. Its arm swung at the shoulder. He pulled its head off — pop! — and set it onto a different body.

"You can SWAP them?" Milo gasped.

"Heads, hats, everything," said the guide. "Mix and match forever."

Milo scanned a bin of tiny hats and found a round, smiling one. He popped it onto a minifigure. "Pretend this one loves sharks, just like me," he said.

Juno found a hat with little bumps and perched it on another minifigure's head. "Pretend this one loves dinosaurs. Just like me!"

The two minifigures stood side by side on the table, hats swapped, grinning their tiny painted grins.

"Every single one is different," Juno said happily, "just like us."

The glowing brick buzzed, warm and bright, as if it liked that answer best of all.

"One more stop," said the guide, smiling, "and then home to bed."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Home Again
chapters.text:
The glowing brick spun faster, flashing gold, green, gold, like a speedy picture show.

"Keep up!" laughed the guide, standing now in a room full of kids just like Milo and Juno, building everywhere.

"In **1999**," said the guide, "LEGO made its first **Star Wars** toy sets." Tiny spaceships zoomed past on a shelf.

"In **2014**," the guide went on, "LEGO characters even starred in their very own movie, in theaters everywhere."

Juno pointed at a kind-looking man grinning at a brick castle. "Who's that?"

"**Kjeld**," said the guide. "Ole Kirk's grandson. He grew up playing with these very bricks, and he took charge of the company in **1979**. His family still owns most of it today."

"And it's all still in Billund?" Milo asked.

"Same ground," said the guide, "where Ole Kirk's little workshop once stood."

Milo pulled the glowing brick from his pocket and pressed it onto one of the very first bricks on a nearby shelf.

**CLICK.**

It fit perfectly.

"Still the same tubes," Milo whispered.

WHOOOOSH! The room melted into swirling color again.

THUMP. They landed on soft carpet. Their own carpet. Milo's tower stood tall beside Juno's toppled dinosaur, right where they'd left them.

The brick in Milo's hand gave one last happy hum, then went still and quiet, one tiny stud still glinting gold.

Juno yawned a dinosaur-sized yawn. "Can we visit again tomorrow?"

"I bet we will," Milo whispered back, tucking the brick safely under his pillow.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: Ole Kirk was a carpenter in **Billund, Denmark**, who started making wooden toys in **1932**.
He named his company **LEGO**, short for the Danish words **leg godt**, which mean **play well**.
People say the word lego also meant **I put together** in an old language far away — but that's probably just a funny accident, not the real reason for the name.
In **1947**, LEGO got one of the first machines in Denmark that could squish melted plastic into toy shapes.
In **1949**, LEGO made its first plastic bricks, called **Automatic Binding Bricks** — but they didn't click together very well yet.
In **1958**, Godtfred added little **tubes** underneath the bricks, so they finally clicked and held tight.
A brick made in **1958** still clicks perfectly with bricks made today.
The first **LEGOLAND** park opened in **Billund** in **1968**, right next to the old factory.
**DUPLO** bricks, sized just right for little hands, came out in **1969** — and they still fit with regular bricks.
The first tiny LEGO people, called **minifigures**, showed up in **1978**, with arms that swing and hats you can swap.
Ole Kirk's grandson **Kjeld** grew up playing with LEGO bricks and took charge of the company in **1979**.
LEGO made its first **Star Wars** toy sets in **1999**.
In **2014**, LEGO characters starred in their very own movie.

story.title: Theo and the First Game Ever Made
story.subtitle: A midnight trip through sixty years of video games, one glitch at a time.

chapters.heading: Level 1: Two Dots and a Line (1958)
chapters.text:
Theo's fort wasn't blankets anymore — it was a glowing laptop, three pillows, and total midnight silence. He was testing bounce physics for his new Roblox soccer game, the one where the ball was supposed to curve around defenders like a real free kick.

It wasn't curving. It was flopping sideways like a dead fish.

"Come ON," Theo muttered, nudging a slider in Roblox Studio for the ninth time.

The screen flickered. Not a glitch-flicker — a real one, black with thin green lines scribbling across it like a heart monitor gone haywire. A single green dot blinked awake in the corner and waved.

"NEW PLAYER HAS JOINED," it said, in a voice like an old dial-up modem learning to talk. "Name's Blip. You wanna know who invented bounce physics? Follow me."

Before Theo could ask what that meant, the green lines snapped into shape: a net, a court, two little dashes acting as paddles.

"That's not a net," Theo said. "That's... weirdly exactly a net."

"Good eye," said Blip. "In **1958**, a scientist named **William Higinbotham** built this at a science lab called **Brookhaven National Laboratory**. He called it Tennis for Two. It ran on an **oscilloscope** — a round screen scientists used to watch wobbly lines, kind of like the machines that beep next to hospital beds."

Theo leaned closer. The ball — one glowing dot — arced over the net and dropped with actual weight, actual gravity, the same thing his Roblox ball refused to do.

"Wait," said Theo. "His ball curves because of gravity. Mine's just... sliding."

"So fix it," said Blip.

Theo reached for the glowing dial — it felt like turning a volume knob — and nudged it. The ball's arc deepened, dropped, bounced true.

**WHOOOOSH.** The whole green screen lit up like a scoreboard.

"IT BOUNCES!" Theo yelled, loud enough that he clapped a hand over his own mouth and glanced at his closed door.

Blip didn't seem worried. "First game in history," he said, "and you just debugged it. Ready for Level Two?"

The green lines folded up like paper and swallowed the room whole.

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Fridge-Sized Computer (1962)
chapters.text:
The green lines snapped back together into a new picture: a dark screen dotted with stars, two tiny spaceships drifting in slow circles.

"Welcome to a computer room so big you could practically bike through it," said Blip. "This is **MIT**, **1962**. A student named **Steve Russell** and his friends wrote a game on a computer called the **PDP-1** — back then, one computer could fill an entire wall of a room."

Theo stared at the two ships. "Spacewar," he read off a flickering label. "Why's it called that if nothing's exploding?"

"Give it a second," said Blip.

One ship fired a dot. It missed, curving the wrong way, the same floppy arc Theo knew way too well from his own unfinished soccer game.

"That's the gravity star pulling it off course," Blip said, pointing to a bright dot glowing at the center of the screen. "Real physics. Same kind of fix you already made once tonight."

Theo grabbed the stick — it clicked like an old joystick, stiff and satisfying under his thumb, nothing like the smooth sliders in Roblox Studio. He nudged the thrust, angling the ship the way he'd angle a free kick: not at the target, but at where the target was *about* to be.

**PEW.** The shot curved clean around the gravity star and tagged the other ship dead center.

"That's basically a bent corner kick," Theo said, grinning so wide it hurt.

"You just out-coded two MIT students at one in the morning," said Blip. "Ready to see what happens when somebody tries to get this out of the lab and onto a television at home?"

"Wait — people didn't have this at home?"

"Nobody did," Blip said. "Yet."

The stars folded into a fridge-sized blur and vanished.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Brown Box and the Ping (1972)
chapters.text:
The blur became a cluttered garage: wires everywhere, a wooden box taped to a tiny TV, a man hunched over it with a screwdriver.

"This fella's got the right idea," said Blip, nodding at the man. "**Ralph Baer**. Folks later called him 'the father of video games.' Back in the late 1960s, he built this — the **Brown Box** — so people could play games on their own television at home, not just on some giant lab machine."

Theo peered at the screen: two white rectangles and a single square bouncing between them. "That's... Pong? Before Pong?"

"Smart kid. In **1972**, Baer's box became the **Magnavox Odyssey** — the first home video game console ever sold." Blip paused like he was savoring it. "Same year, two guys named **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started a company called **Atari** and put their own version of the game in arcades. They called it **Pong**."

The garage dissolved into neon: a dim arcade, one glowing cabinet in the corner, a crowd of fuzzy figures waiting their turn.

"People went nuts for this thing," Blip said. "Story goes, one machine got so stuffed with quarters it actually jammed shut. Might be a bit of a tall tale — but it tells you how fast this game caught on."

Theo stepped up to the cabinet. The paddle control was just a dial, nothing like his Roblox control scheme, and his first shot sailed wide.

"Think goalie," Blip said. "Watch the ball, not the dial."

Theo squinted, tracked the white square's bounce, and turned the knob at the last second like he was diving to save a penalty. **CLICK. PING!** The ball cracked back across the screen and the crowd of fuzzy figures cheered.

"First home console, and the arcade hit that built a whole company," said Blip, "both from one single year. Not bad for 1972."

"IT WORKS ON MY OWN TV!" Theo shouted, then clapped a hand over his mouth, even though there was no TV anywhere near his bedroom anymore — just green light swallowing the arcade whole.
chapters.shout_line: IT WORKS ON MY OWN TV!

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Click of a Cartridge (1977–1978)
chapters.text:
The green light settled into a den with shag carpet and a boxy console under the TV, a stack of plastic rectangles beside it.

"**1977**," said Blip. "The **Atari 2600**. Before this, a console only played whatever game was built right into it. This one took **cartridges** — plastic cases you could pop in and swap out, so one machine could play a whole pile of different games."

Theo turned one over in his hands. "So it's like... downloading a new game, except it's a brick."

"Basically," said Blip. "Pick one."

Theo slid a cartridge in. **CLICK.** The screen filled with rows of blocky aliens, marching side to side, inching slowly down toward him.

"**1978**," Blip said. "A designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado** made this one for a company called **Taito**. **Space Invaders.** It kicked off an arcade craze across the whole world — lines out the door, pockets full of coins, kids skipping dinner to play one more round."

The aliens sped up every time a row vanished, same as Theo's own Roblox enemies always did when his difficulty settings panicked and buffed everything at once.

"They're bunched like a bad defensive line," Theo muttered, studying the formation. "If I pick off the edges first, the middle collapses slower instead of swarming me."

He fired at the outer columns, saving the center for last. The rows thinned out evenly instead of caving all at once, and his little cannon survived three full waves before the screen flashed a victory green.

"Nobody's cracked that pattern on their first try in years," said Blip, sounding almost impressed. "You've basically been coding boss fights your whole life."

"I mean," Theo said, "yeah. Kind of. That's literally what I do at eleven p.m. on a Tuesday."

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Pizza With a Bite Out of It (1980–1983)
chapters.text:
The arcade cabinet in front of them glowed bright yellow, a hungry little circle gobbling dots down a maze.

"**1980**," Blip said. "Designer **Toru Iwatani** made this one for a company called **Namco**. **Pac-Man.** Story goes he dreamed it up looking at a pizza with a slice missing — though nobody's totally sure that's really how it happened."

"A pizza," Theo repeated. "He invented one of the most famous games ever because he was hungry."

"Possibly," said Blip. "Still a great game either way."

Theo took the joystick, cornered a ghost right after grabbing a power pellet, and gobbled it clean. The screen chirped happily, a tidy little victory.

Then the arcade flickered and dimmed, color draining out of it like a bad render.

"What happened?" Theo asked.

"**1983**," said Blip, voice dropping gentler. "So many companies rushed out sloppy, half-finished games that stores got stuffed with stuff nobody wanted to buy anymore. The whole video game business in North America shrank — fast. People called it the crash."

The screen showed rows of unsold cartridges, boxed up, trucked away somewhere.

"There's a story," Blip went on, "that a pile of unsold cartridges — including one based on the movie E.T. — got buried in a landfill out in New Mexico. People actually dug the spot up and found them there in **2014**, so that part, at least, turned out true."

Theo crouched by the flickering pile. "So the industry basically shipped a bad patch and had to roll back the whole update."

"That's exactly what happened," said Blip. "Took somebody clever to patch it properly."

"Who?"

The green light pulled tight, folding toward a new year stamped in the corner of the screen: **1985**.

chapters.heading: Level 6: Falling Blocks and a Jumping Plumber (1984–1985)
chapters.text:
The green light landed in a plain office, one glowing computer screen humming in the corner.

"**1984**," said Blip. "**Moscow**. A scientist named **Alexey Pajitnov** built a puzzle where blocks of different shapes fall and you've got to fit them together perfectly. **Tetris.**"

Blocks rained down the screen. Theo caught the rhythm fast — he'd stacked a thousand blocky structures in Roblox Studio for fun, snapping shapes into tight grids until nothing wasted space.

"This is just building, but it's yelling at you," Theo said, rotating an L-shaped piece and sliding it flush against the wall. A full row lit up and vanished with a satisfying hum.

"Most satisfying sound in gaming history, some people say," Blip said. "Keep going — we're due in **1985**."

The office melted into a cartoon kingdom: green pipes, red brick blocks, a mustached plumber standing at the edge of a cliff.

"The crash scared a lot of people out of the console business," said Blip. "Then Nintendo showed up with the **NES**, and bundled it with this guy."

"Mario," Theo said instantly. "Everyone knows Mario."

"**Shigeru Miyamoto** designed him in **1985**," said Blip. "Turns out a jumping plumber was exactly what the whole business needed to get back on its feet."

Theo grabbed the controller and lined up Mario's jump the way he'd line up a header — watch the arc, time the peak, never rush it. He cleared the gap, stomped a mushroom creature flat, and the screen chimed a little victory tune.

"Ten out of ten hitbox," Theo said approvingly. "Whoever tuned this jump knew exactly what they were doing."

"The whole industry thought so too," said Blip. "This is the game that brought it back from the dead."

chapters.heading: Level 7: Blue Blurs and Shiny Discs (1991–1994)
chapters.text:
The scene snapped into motion so fast Theo nearly lost his balance: loops, rings, a blue blur rocketing past.

"**1991**," Blip said. "**Sega** needed a hero fast enough to race Nintendo's plumber. So they made **Sonic the Hedgehog** — built for speed, blue, plenty of attitude."

Theo grabbed the controller and Sonic rocketed into a loop, rings scattering like confetti. "This feels like sprinting a counterattack," Theo said, timing a jump off a ramp mid-sprint. "You don't stop to think, you just read the field."

"Exactly the idea," said Blip. "Keep moving — **1994** now."

The loops folded into a sleek gray console, a silver disc spinning inside it.

"**Sony** jumped into consoles with the **PlayStation**," Blip said. "It used **CDs** instead of cartridges, which meant way more room for video and sound — games started looking and sounding almost like actual movies."

Theo popped the disc case open and closed it, oddly satisfying, like opening a little treasure chest with real hinges.

The console scene dimmed, and new light flickered on: a cluttered room full of kids and clunky computers, thick cables running between every machine like spaghetti.

"**1993**," Blip said. "A game called **Doom** got people doing this — hauling their whole computer over to a friend's house and wiring all the machines together so everyone could play at once. People called it a **LAN party** — hooking up a bunch of computers in one room so you could all play together."

"That's basically a server," Theo said, grinning. "They just built it out of extension cords."

"Pretty much," Blip said. "You've been doing this with friends online for years. They had to physically drag their whole setup across town just to manage it."

Theo laughed, picturing it: ten kids, ten monitors, one single multiplayer match, and somebody definitely tripping over a cable.

chapters.heading: Level 8: Home (2006–2015)
chapters.text:
The LAN party dissolved, and the green light swept Theo into a living room full of people waving their arms at a TV, no buttons being mashed, just motion.

"**2006**," Blip said. "The **Wii**. Nintendo put a motion sensor in the controller, so you swing it like a real bat or racket instead of pressing buttons. Grandparents who'd never touched a console in their life lined up to try it."

Theo swung an imaginary tennis racket and watched the on-screen swing match his, half a second behind. "That's wild," he said. "No buttons, just... moving."

"Last stop," said Blip, and the living room crumbled into blocky green hills, blocky trees, a blocky sun.

"Wait, I know this," Theo said immediately.

"**2011**," said Blip. "A Swedish developer named **Markus Persson** — people called him **Notch** — released this one. **Minecraft.** It later became the best-selling video game ever made."

"I have genuinely built forty houses in this exact art style," Theo said, picking up a blocky dirt square like it personally owed him something.

The blocky hills folded away gently this time, not snapping — almost like the story was winding down on purpose.

"One more thing," Blip said. The green light settled into a quiet museum hallway, glass cases glowing softly. "**2015**. A place called the **World Video Game Hall of Fame** opened in a museum called **The Strong**, in **Rochester, New York**. Pac-Man's in there. Mario. Tetris. Pong. All of it."

"All the stuff from tonight," Theo said quietly.

"All the stuff that got us to you," said Blip, "sitting on your floor at midnight, fixing a soccer ball's curve."

The green lines folded up one final time, soft as a page turning, and the glow pulled back into Theo's own laptop screen, exactly where it had started — except now the slider in Roblox Studio sat fixed, the ball's arc curving clean and true all the way across the pitch.

Theo blinked at his own game, suddenly working perfectly.

"Blip?" he whispered.

No answer. Just a tiny green dot in the corner of the screen, blinking once, like a wink, before it faded out completely.

Theo saved his file, closed the laptop, and lay back grinning in the dark.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a whole game left to build.

story.title: Milo, Juno, and the Brick That Found Sharks
story.subtitle: A splashy swim through the oldest hunters in the sea.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Older Than Dinosaurs
chapters.text:
Milo sat on his bedroom floor, snapping red bricks onto a half-built shark. Juno marched a tiny dinosaur across the carpet beside him. The tower from last week's adventure still stood in the corner. It had held together all week, every single brick.

Milo pressed one more brick onto his shark's fin. The brick began to glow. Then it went CLICK.

"Juno, look!" Milo whispered. The glow grew brighter, like a tiny sun.

WHOOOOSH! The room spun. When it stopped, Milo and Juno were floating in deep blue water, bubbles all around them.

"Where are we?" asked Juno, hugging her dinosaur tight.

A long gray shape swam close, its tail swishing side to side.

"That is a shark," said Milo. "I know sharks!"

The shark's skeleton was not hard like Milo's LEGO bricks. It was soft and bendy, like the squishy part of your ear.

"Sharks have bendy bones," Milo said, "instead of hard ones."

"And sharks swam here," the brick hummed, "before your dinosaurs, Juno. Before trees, even."

Juno gasped. "Before dinosaurs?"

"Way before," the brick said. "More than four hundred million years ago."

Juno looked at her tiny dinosaur toy. "You are not as old as sharks," she told it, patting its head.

Milo laughed so hard he blew bubbles.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Tooth That Fell Like Snow
chapters.text:
A huge gray shark swam close. Its mouth was full of pointy teeth.

Milo's eyes went wide. "Is that a great white shark?"

"Yes," hummed the brick. "Great white sharks grow up to **twenty feet long**."

"Whoa," said Juno. "That is so, so long!"

Milo watched the shark glide by. He stayed back, just watching, the way you watch a big dog you don't know.

A tiny white tooth floated down, like a snowflake. Milo caught it in his hand.

"Sharks lose teeth all the time," said the brick. "**New teeth just move forward** to take their place."

"So he's not missing it?" Milo asked.

"Nope," said the brick. "He probably has a thousand more waiting in line."

Juno touched the tooth's edge. "It feels bumpy!"

"Shark skin is bumpy too," said the brick. "Tiny tooth-shaped bumps cover it. That makes it feel **rough, like sandpaper**."

Milo rubbed his own arm. "Not like my skin!"

"Only shark skin," laughed the brick.

Milo tucked the tooth into his pocket. "Souvenir," he said proudly.

"TEENY BUMPS!" Juno shouted, patting the water like it might be bumpy too.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Biggest, Gentlest Mouth
chapters.text:
Something enormous slid out of the blue. It was bigger than their whole house.

Juno froze. "Is it going to eat us?"

"No, no," said the brick quickly. "That is a whale shark. It only eats teeny tiny bits of food."

Juno breathed out. "Phew."

"This big fish is the **biggest fish in the whole world**," the brick said. "But it only eats tiny floaty bits, by gulping water through its giant mouth."

Milo looked up at it, way up. "That's the biggest giant gulp ever."

Juno spread her arms as wide as they would go. "Was its mouth THIS big?"

"Even bigger," said the brick.

Juno spread her arms wider, wobbling, and Milo caught her before she tipped over.

"Careful!" he said, grinning.

The whale shark swam on, slow and calm, like it had nowhere to be.

"Some whale sharks live to be **one hundred years old**," said the brick. "Maybe older than your grandma."

"That's old!" said Juno, waving at it from far away. "Bye, old fish! Swim well!"

The giant shark gave one slow swish of its tail and disappeared into the blue.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Giant from Long Ago
chapters.text:
The water turned a deeper blue. Milo felt a little shiver.

"Is something scary down there?" he asked.

"Not anymore," said the brick gently. "There used to be a shark here called **Megalodon**. He was one of the biggest sharks ever."

"Is he still down there?" Juno asked, grabbing Milo's hand.

"No," said the brick. "Megalodon is **extinct** now. That means every single one of them is gone, and none are left anywhere. He swam a long, long time ago."

Milo relaxed. "So we're safe."

"Totally safe," said the brick.

Something pale sat on the sandy floor. Milo scooped it up. It was a tooth as big as his whole hand.

"Whoa!" said Milo. "Is this his tooth?"

"Yes," said the brick. "We mostly know about Megalodon from teeth like that one. They turned into **fossils** — that means they got left in the ground so long they turned hard as rock, and that's how scientists found them."

Juno patted her tiny dinosaur. "You missed him by a lot."

Milo set the giant tooth back down carefully. "Goodbye, giant shark. You were probably awesome."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Hammers and Walking Fins
chapters.text:
A strange shape swam past. Its head was wide and flat, like a hammer.

"That shark's head looks silly!" Juno giggled.

"That is a hammerhead shark," said the brick. "Its wide head spreads its eyes apart, so it can see **all around itself**, almost like a wraparound window."

Milo tried spreading his hands out by his own ears, pretending to be a hammerhead. "Can you see me, Juno?"

"I see you being silly," Juno laughed.

Then something even stranger happened. A small spotted shark flip-flopped across the sandy floor using its fins like little paddles.

"Is it... walking?" Milo asked.

"That's an epaulette shark," said the brick. "It can **walk across the sand** on its fins, from one tide pool to another."

Juno plopped down and flip-flopped her hands like fins. "Look, I'm walking like a shark!"

Milo flip-flopped beside her, and they both wiggled across an invisible floor, giggling until bubbles streamed from their mouths.

"WALKING SHARK!" Juno shouted, and the little shark seemed to wiggle one fin back at them before paddling off into the reef.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Fast, Rivery, and Resting
chapters.text:
A silvery shark zoomed past so fast it left bubbles swirling behind it.

"WHOOOOSH!" shouted Juno. "That one's fast!"

"That's a mako shark," said the brick. "It's the **fastest shark** there is, zooming to catch its dinner."

Milo tried to swim after it and only managed a wobbly paddle. "Nope. Too fast for me."

Next, they floated near the edge of a river flowing into the sea. A shark swam right where the salty water met the fresh water.

"Sharks don't go in rivers... do they?" Milo asked.

"Bull sharks do," said the brick. "They can swim in salty ocean water **and** in rivers."

On the sandy floor below, a shark lay very still, barely moving.

"Is it sleeping?" Juno whispered.

"Resting," said the brick. "That's a nurse shark. It can **pump water over its gills** while it rests, so it doesn't have to keep swimming just to breathe."

Then Milo spotted something odd caught in some seaweed — a dark, leathery little pouch.

"What's this?"

"A mermaid's purse," said the brick. "Some sharks lay eggs inside cases just like that one."

"A purse for a baby shark," Milo said softly, and set it gently back in the seaweed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Shark Lady and the Way Home
chapters.text:
A kind-looking diver swam past, smiling at them through her mask.

"Who's that?" Juno asked.

"That's **Eugenie Clark**," said the brick. "People called her the Shark Lady. She studied sharks for years and years, and showed everyone that sharks are curious, and can even learn tricks."

Milo waved, and the diver waved right back before swimming off into the blue.

"There are more than **five hundred kinds of sharks** in the ocean," the brick said, "and we only met a few tonight."

"Five hundred!" Milo said. "We need way more bedtimes."

"Sharks help keep the ocean healthy," said the brick. "They're at the **very top**, which keeps everything underneath them just right."

Juno yawned a huge yawn, bubbles drifting up from her mouth.

"Time to go home," said the brick. It began to glow, bright as a tiny sun.

WHOOOOSH! The water spun away. Milo and Juno landed softly on their bedroom carpet, right beside their tall LEGO tower.

Milo checked his pocket. The little white tooth was still there, resting next to the tower that had held all week.

"Souvenir," he whispered, setting it carefully on the carpet.

Juno hugged her dinosaur tight. "Sharks are older than you," she told it again, "but you're still my favorite."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well, little sharks.

story.title: Theo and the Soccer Game That Never Ends
story.subtitle: Nine levels, one ball, two thousand years of kicking it around

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Kicking Game of Han China
chapters.text:
Theo's screen glowed in the dark long after lights-out. He'd spent an hour tweaking the goal zone in his new Roblox soccer map, trying to make the net wobble just right when a ball hit it.

A week had passed since the words THE NEXT LEVEL IS YOURS TO BUILD had faded off his monitor. Tonight he was finally building — right up until the screen flickered green and black.

**BZZZT.**

A tiny square figure dropped into the corner of the screen, pixels stacking like bricks. "Player One," squeaked Bit. "You built a goal. Want to see where the whole game started?"

"Soccer doesn't have a start screen, Bit. It's just soccer."

"Wrong load screen," Bit said. "Every game has an origin level. Yours goes back more than two thousand years."

The bedroom dissolved into bright banners and a dusty courtyard. Men in wrapped tunics juggled a round ball off their feet, knees, and shoulders, never once touching it with their hands.

"Welcome to Han China," Bit said. "This game is called **cuju** — 'kickball.' People have played it here for over **2,000 years**."

Theo watched a player flick the ball up, catch it on his shoulder, then nod it to a teammate. "That's basically keepie-uppies," he said. "We do that at practice."

"Same instinct," Bit said. "People wanted to kick a ball into a target long before anyone wrote the rules down."

Theo spotted a gap in the compound wall shaped exactly like a hoop. He pointed. "Is that the goal?"

"Good eye, Player One. Score through there and the level's done."

Theo grabbed a loose ball rolling toward him, lined up his foot the way his coach had taught him, and struck it clean through the gap.

**WHOOSH.**

The courtyard roared in a language Theo didn't understand but didn't need to. A single gold coin popped out of the hoop and spun into his open hand.

"Level complete," Bit said, voice going warm and crackly. "One coin, one level. Keep playing."

"How many levels are there?" Theo asked.

"Funny you should ask," Bit said, already pulling up the next one.

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Game That Got Banned (1314)
chapters.text:
A leather ball cannoned off a bakery stall and nearly flattened a chicken. Theo ducked just in time.

The street was pure chaos — dozens of men shoving, grabbing, and occasionally kicking something vaguely ball-shaped toward two goals a mile apart.

"Welcome to medieval England," Bit said, hovering at shoulder height. "They call this mob football. No ref. No rules. Just... everyone."

"This is not soccer practice," Theo said, watching a man get knocked flat, pop back up laughing, and keep running.

"No kidding," Bit said. "It got so out of hand that in **1314**, **King Edward II** banned it in London. Said it caused too much chaos in the streets."

Theo grinned. "A king banned soccer for being too much fun?"

"Pretty much. Didn't stop anyone. People just played somewhere the king couldn't see."

Theo spotted a quieter side alley where a few boys were actually passing the ball, aiming instead of just grabbing. He pointed it out. "That's what this game needs. Rules."

"Good read, Player One," Bit said. "Rules are coming. Just not yet."

A gold coin dropped into Theo's palm, buzzing faintly. "Level complete," Bit said, "even though technically nobody followed a single law to earn it."

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Ball in the Castle Wall
chapters.text:
Workers prying open an old stone wall found something round and leathery wedged behind a beam. Theo leaned in close.

"It's a ball," Bit said. "Found for real, hidden in the rafters of **Stirling Castle** in Scotland. Some think it's been there since the **1540s**."

Theo turned it over as Bit blew the image up bigger. The ball was made from a bladder — Bit explained that meant the stretchy balloon part inside an animal, blown up and wrapped in leather panels to hold its round shape.

"So that's basically a four-hundred-year-old soccer ball," Theo said.

"The oldest one anyone's ever found," Bit said. "Nobody's sure exactly who played with it. But it's real, and it's old, and that's a pretty good combo."

Theo noticed loose stitching along one seam, ready to burst. He pinched it carefully shut, the same way he patched the torn practice net back home.

**CLICK.** The seam held.

"Nice hands," Bit said. "Also — please don't actually touch four-hundred-year-old artifacts. That one's pretend."

Theo laughed as a third coin dropped into his pocket, buzzing softly. "Level complete."

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Cambridge Rules (1848)
chapters.text:
Two students were nearly shouting over a chalkboard. Theo had never seen homework get this heated.

"Every school's got different rules!" one yelled. "Mine lets you catch the ball. Yours doesn't!"

"We need ONE set everyone agrees on," the other snapped, scribbling fast.

Bit zoomed in. "**Cambridge University**, **1848**. Students from different schools, each with their own version of football, trying to write down one rulebook everybody could actually play by. They called it the **Cambridge Rules**."

Theo studied the chalkboard, half-finished and crossed out everywhere. "They can't agree on anything."

"That's exactly the problem," Bit said. "Every school had basically invented its own soccer."

Theo grabbed a spare piece of chalk and added one line at the bottom, copying what he always did for his own Roblox rulebook: NO HANDS. CLEAR GOAL ZONES. ONE SET OF RULES FOR EVERYONE.

Both students stopped arguing and stared at it. One nodded slowly and copied it onto the real board.

"Did I just help write actual history?" Theo asked.

"You wrote a rule that was basically already arriving," Bit said. "But yeah. Nice timing."

A fourth coin spun into Theo's hand. "Level complete."

chapters.heading: Level 5: The FA Is Born (1863)
chapters.text:
Candles flickered over a long table crowded with serious men in suits. Theo had wandered into the world's most boring-looking birthday party.

"This is **London**, **October 26, 1863**," Bit said. "They're founding the **Football Association** — the FA. Rule one on the table tonight: no more carrying the ball with your hands."

A tall man near the head of the table wrote fast, ink smudging his fingers. "That's **Ebenezer Cobb Morley**," Bit said. "He's about to write the first official **Laws of the Game** — soccer's rulebook. The same one still followed today."

Theo peered over Morley's shoulder at a half-finished rule about handling the ball. "So before tonight, people could just pick it up?"

"Some clubs let you," Bit said. "Tonight that stops, for good."

Morley's pen hovered, stuck on a word. Theo leaned in. "Call it association football," he suggested, remembering something Bit had mentioned earlier. "Short for—"

"—'assoc,'" Bit finished. "Which is exactly where the word **soccer** came from. British schoolboys shortened it themselves, in the **1880s**."

Morley wrote the word down and kept going, satisfied.

Theo grinned. "I just helped name my own sport."

"Debatable," Bit said, "but I'll allow it." A fifth coin landed in Theo's palm, still warm from the candlelight. "Level complete."

chapters.heading: Level 6: First Cup, First Clash
chapters.text:
A cheer rattled through a packed wooden grandstand. Theo had never seen a trophy that small get carried so carefully.

"**1871-72**," Bit said. "The first ever **FA Cup**. Oldest football competition still running anywhere in the world."

Theo watched two teams shake hands at midfield, mud up to their knees. "It's still around? Like, still being handed out?"

"Every single year since," Bit said. "Some trophies retire. This one just kept going."

Bit flicked the scene forward a few months. Bigger crowd now, flags waving in two colors. "**1872**, Glasgow," Bit said. "First official international match ever played. **Scotland versus England**."

Both teams defended like their lives depended on it. Ninety minutes later, the scoreboard still read nothing to nothing.

"Zero-zero?" Theo said. "That's the big historic game?"

"Sometimes history's a draw," Bit said. "Nobody lost. Nobody won. Everybody still showed up and made it count."

Theo thought about his own team's scoreless games, the ones that felt pointless at the final whistle. This one didn't feel pointless at all.

"PLAYED FOR REAL!" Theo yelled, startling a flag-waving fan in a top hat.

A sixth coin landed in his hand, humming. "Level complete," said Bit.

chapters.heading: Level 7: Leagues and a World Body
chapters.text:
A man with ink-stained fingers was circling team names on a huge map of England. Theo peeked over his shoulder.

"**William McGregor**, **1888**," Bit said. "He's organizing the **Football League** — the world's first league where teams play each other on a real, fixed schedule."

"So before this, teams just played whoever, whenever?" Theo asked.

"Pretty much," Bit said. "McGregor's the one who said: let's make a proper table. Standings. A real season."

Theo traced one of McGregor's pencil lines, stretching it to connect two teams that weren't linked yet. McGregor glanced down, frowned, then redrew it exactly how Theo had traced it.

"I did not just fix English football scheduling," Theo whispered.

"You absolutely did," Bit said, already pulling up the next scene. Paris now, a smaller room, seven men signing a single sheet of paper. "**1904**," Bit said. "Seven countries founding **FIFA** — the organization that still runs soccer's rules worldwide."

Theo counted the signatures. "Seven countries? That's it?"

"Everyone else joined later," Bit said. "You've gotta start somewhere."

A seventh coin dropped into Theo's hand, buzzing like it couldn't decide on one accent. "Level complete."

chapters.heading: Level 8: The World Cup Speedrun
chapters.text:
Confetti rained from nowhere. Bit grinned so hard his pixels wobbled.

"Buckle up, Player One. This level moves fast."

The world blurred into a packed stadium in South America. "**1930**," Bit said. "First ever **World Cup**. Host country **Uruguay** beat **Argentina** in the final."

A stocky man lifted a small golden statue, grinning harder than the trophy itself. "**Jules Rimet**," Bit said. "He's the one who pushed for a whole World Cup to happen. They named the original trophy after him."

Before Theo could ask anything, the scene jumped. London, gray sky, a glass display case — empty.

"**1966**," Bit said. "Someone stole the World Cup trophy right out of its case. A whole week, nobody could find it."

Theo's stomach dropped. "Did they get it back?"

"Found safe," Bit said, "by a dog. A terrier. Named **Pickles**. Sniffed it out wrapped in newspaper under a hedge."

"A DOG FOUND THE WORLD CUP!" Theo yelled.

"Best detective in football history," Bit said. "That same year, **England** hosted the tournament — and won it. Their only title so far."

The scene jumped again — a referee holding up a small bright rectangle. "**1970**," Bit said. "First time anyone used **yellow and red cards**. An official named **Ken Aston** got the idea from a traffic light — stop at red, slow down at yellow."

Theo pointed at a player getting flashed yellow after a clumsy foul. "That's basically a warning light for cheating."

"Exactly," Bit said.

One more jump: a trophy case, a new golden statue spinning slowly, a different shape than before. "**Brazil** kept that first trophy for good, after winning their third title," Bit said. "Won it **five times** total — more than anyone else. So in **1974**, FIFA made a brand new trophy for everyone else to compete over."

Theo squinted at a grainy clip of a player weaving past three defenders like they were practice cones. "Who's that?"

"**Pele**," Bit said. "Only player ever on three different World Cup-winning teams — **1958**, **1962**, **1970**. All with Brazil."

Theo watched the move loop. "I'm stealing that for my Roblox game."

"Please don't make the ball sentient," Bit said. "Last time was a disaster."

A whole fistful of coins dropped into Theo's hands at once, one for every decade Bit had just blown through. "Level complete. Several times over."
chapters.shout_line: A DOG FOUND THE WORLD CUP!

chapters.heading: Level 9: The Lionesses Who Wouldn't Stop
chapters.text:
Fifty thousand people roared in a stadium that was supposedly just hosting a friendly match. Theo blinked at the size of the crowd.

"**England**, early 1900s," Bit said. "This is the **Dick, Kerr Ladies**, one of the most popular football teams in the whole country. That forward scoring from everywhere — that's **Lily Parr**."

Theo watched Parr blast a shot past a diving goalkeeper. "She's incredible. Why haven't I heard of her?"

Bit's pixels dimmed a shade. "Because in **1921**, the people running English football banned women from playing on their fields. Didn't matter how good anyone was."

Theo frowned hard. "That's not fair. That's not fair at all."

"No," Bit agreed. "It wasn't. It took fifty years — until **1971** — for that ban to finally get lifted."

The scene shifted, bright and loud, a tournament now. "**1991**, China," Bit said. "First ever official **Women's World Cup**. The **United States** won it."

Theo watched the American team pile on top of each other, trophy held high. He thought about his own team, half the starting lineup girls who could outplay him on a good day.

"They should've just let Lily Parr play the whole time," Theo said quietly.

"Agreed," Bit said. "But once that door opened back up, nobody was shutting it again."

Theo held his hand out before the coin even dropped, like he already knew it was coming. It landed anyway, buzzing louder than the others. "Level complete," Bit said. "That one mattered."

chapters.heading: Level 10: Build Your Own Field
chapters.text:
The green flicker faded. Theo's bedroom snapped back into focus — same messy carpet, same glowing monitor, same half-finished goal net wobbling on his Roblox map.

Nine coins sat warm in his hand, humming together like they were trying to finish a song.

"Go on," Bit said, voice doing that crackly, watery thing it always did near the end. "You know how this works."

Theo set the coins in a circle on his desk. They melted together, pixel by pixel, into one small glowing trophy — rounder than the first one, newer than the last.

"Two thousand years," Theo said, turning it over in his hands. "From a guy in China kicking a ball through a gap in a wall, to a dog finding a stolen trophy, to actual rules finally letting everyone play."

"That's the whole game," Bit said. "Still being played. Still getting written."

Theo looked at his half-built goal net glowing on the screen, the one he'd been tweaking for an hour before any of this started. He nudged the wobble setting one more time. It looked right now.

A message blinked onto the screen: YOU FOUND THE WHOLE FIELD. NOW BUILD YOUR OWN.

Bit's eyes went small and glassy, like a screen losing signal for just a second. "Night, Player One," he said. "Go build something good."

Then the pixels folded in on themselves, and the room was just a room again — ball, net, and a kid with a new trophy and a better idea for his goal.

story.ending_line: Saturday's game couldn't come soon enough — and neither could the next build.

true_facts.text: **Cuju**, a kickball game played in Han China, started more than **2,000 years ago**.
Medieval 'mob football' got so wild that **King Edward II** banned it in London in **1314**.
Cambridge University students wrote the **Cambridge Rules** in **1848**, trying to make one rulebook everyone could follow.
The **Football Association** was founded in **London** on **October 26, 1863**, and banned players from picking up the ball with their hands.
**Ebenezer Cobb Morley** personally wrote the first official **Laws of the Game** that same night.
The word **soccer** comes from 'assoc' — British schoolboys' short version of 'association football' in the **1880s**.
The **FA Cup**, first played in **1871-72**, is the oldest football competition still running anywhere in the world.
**William McGregor** organized the **Football League** in **1888**, the world's first league with a real schedule.
**FIFA**, soccer's worldwide rule-keeper, was founded in **Paris** in **1904** by seven countries.
The first **World Cup** was played in **Uruguay** in **1930**, with the host team beating **Argentina** in the final.
In **1966** the World Cup trophy was stolen in London — then found safe a week later by a dog named **Pickles**.
Women's football was finally allowed back onto English fields in **1971**, after being banned for fifty years.
The first official **Women's World Cup** was held in **1991** and won by the **United States**.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Theo's nine gold coins fused into a new glowing trophy on his desk, and a message told him to stop exploring soccer's history and go build his own field.

story.title: Juno, Milo, and Theo and the Mountain That Breathes Fire
story.subtitle: A rumbly, glowing journey to the center of a volcano — and back again.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Brick
chapters.text:
Milo lay on his bedroom floor, snapping red and orange LEGO bricks together. He was building a volcano, tall and lumpy, just for fun.

Juno sat beside him, lining up her dinosaurs in a neat row. Theo flopped on the bed, tapping away at a game on his tablet.

Then the little LEGO volcano began to hum. HMMMMM.

Milo froze. "Did it just wiggle?"

The mountain glowed orange from the inside, like a nightlight waking up. POP! A tiny, warm, glowing rock creature hopped out of the top. He had a crackly voice and a wide, friendly smile.

"Hello, hello!" he said. "I'm Rumble. I live inside real volcanoes. Tonight, I'll live inside yours too."

Juno dropped her dinosaur. "Is a volcano a monster?"

"No, no," laughed Rumble. "A **volcano** is just a hole in the ground. Hot melted rock and gas squeeze out of it, like toothpaste out of a tube."

Milo grinned. "A tube! I get it!"

"Want to see a real one?" Rumble asked, his glow growing brighter.

Theo looked up. "Wait — we're really going?"

Milo grabbed Juno's hand before she could answer. The glow swallowed the whole room. WHOOOOSH!

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Magma Soup
chapters.text:
Rumble zoomed them down a glowing tunnel. WHOOOSH!

The walls dripped with orange goo. Milo reached out, careful not to touch.

"Is that paint?" he asked.

"Nope!" said Rumble. "That's **magma** — hot, melted rock, still underground."

"Like melted crayons," said Milo.

"Exactly. Once it squeezes out on top, we call it lava instead."

Theo tapped the rock wall. It had long cracks, like puzzle pieces.

"Why does the ground look broken?" he asked.

"Good eye," said Rumble. "The ground is made of giant pieces, called plates. They float around, slow as a snail. Most volcanoes pop up where two plates push, pull, or slide."

Theo grinned. "Like pushing blocks together in a game."

"Just like that," said Rumble.

Juno wiggled side to side. "I'm a plate! I slide!"

She bumped gently into Milo. He bumped her right back.

"Follow the crack," said Theo. "Let's see where it goes."

They followed the glowing crack deeper into the mountain. The hum grew louder. HMMMMM.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Ring of Fire
chapters.text:
They shot out of the tunnel into starry dark.

Below them floated a giant glowing map, dotted with tiny red sparks.

"Whoa," said Theo. "Those dots look like a horseshoe!"

Rumble nodded. "Good eye! We call it the **Ring of Fire**. It circles the big Pacific Ocean."

Milo counted sparks with his finger. "There's so many!"

"About three out of every four awake volcanoes on Earth live right in that ring," said Rumble.

Theo traced the shape with his finger, just like drawing a line on a map. "It really is a ring!"

Milo spotted one spot glowing brighter than the rest. "Why is that one so sparkly?"

"That's Indonesia," said Rumble. "It has more awake volcanoes than any other country on Earth."

"More than anywhere?" Milo gasped.

"Yep. Lots and lots."

Juno pointed at the map too. "I want a sparkly dinosaur country!"

Everyone laughed. Rumble's glow turned happy gold.

"Hang on tight," he said. "Next stop — Hawaii!"

The map spun beneath them like a plate on a table. WHIRRRL!

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Hawaii Hotspot
chapters.text:
They landed on black, bumpy rock. Steam puffed out of cracks. PFFFT!

"Welcome to Hawaii," said Rumble. "These volcanoes didn't grow at the edge of a plate. They grew over a hotspot — a patch of extra-hot rock, way down deep."

Milo studied the mountain. It was wide and gentle, like his LEGO baseplate.

"That's not pointy like mine," he said, pointing at his shirt, which had a tall cartoon volcano on it.

"Good noticing," said Rumble. "Some volcanoes are wide and gentle, like this one. Others are tall and steep, like a pointy hat."

"Can we see a pointy one too?" Milo asked.

"Maybe later. First, meet Kilauea. It has been fizzing and popping, almost nonstop, for years and years."

Right on cue, orange lava bubbled nearby. BLOOP, BLOOP!

Juno clapped. "It's like soup!"

"And over there," Rumble pointed, "is Mauna Loa. It's the biggest awake volcano on the whole planet."

Theo whistled. "That's huge."

Milo grinned. "I'm building both shapes when I get home."

"Deal," said Rumble, glowing brighter. "Next, somewhere even newer."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: A Brand New Island
chapters.text:
Next they landed on green, chilly ground. The air smelled like rotten eggs. Juno wrinkled her nose. "Ew!"

"That's just Iceland," laughed Rumble. "It sits where two giant plates pull apart, so a little magma sneaks up through the gap."

Out at sea, the water began to bubble and hiss. HISSSSS!

Juno pointed, eyes wide. "Is a baby island being born?"

"You guessed it!" said Rumble. "In **1963**, a brand-new island popped up out of the sea, right near here. They named it Surtsey."

"A baby island," Juno whispered, amazed. "Like a baby dinosaur hatching!"

"Kind of like that," Rumble chuckled.

Theo leaned over the edge. "So the island just grew?"

"Bit by bit," said Rumble. "Lava poured out, cooled into rock, and stacked up until it reached the top of the water."

Juno wanted to watch a little longer. They sat on warm stones and watched the bubbles pop. POP. POP. POP.

"Can we visit it when it's all grown?" Juno asked.

"Someday," said Rumble gently. "For now, let's see a very old, very sleepy one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Sleepy Giant
chapters.text:
They landed on a wide, grassy plain. Steam curled up from little pools nearby. HISSSSS.

"This mountain had one giant eruption, long, long ago," said Rumble. "About **640,000 years ago**."

Juno's eyes went round. "Is it going to erupt — pop and spill out — right NOW?"

"No, no," said Rumble, patting her hand. "Scientists watch it every single day, and they see no sign it will erupt soon."

Theo leaned forward. "How do they watch a whole mountain?"

"With clever tools," said Rumble. "One is called a seismograph — a machine that feels even the tiniest wiggle in the ground."

"Like a doctor's stethoscope, but for Earth," said Theo.

"Exactly like that," said Rumble, impressed.

Milo patted the warm ground. "So it's just sleeping?"

"Just sleeping," said Rumble. "Very, very deeply."

Juno breathed out, relieved, and flopped down in the grass. "Okay. Good. Night night, sleepy mountain."

Everyone giggled.

"Next," said Rumble, "let's go somewhere no human has ever stood."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Biggest Volcano Ever
chapters.text:
WHOOOSH! They zoomed way up, past the clouds, past the moon, until red dust crunched beneath their feet.

"Where are we?" gasped Milo.

"Mars," said Rumble. "Look up."

They tilted their heads back, and back, and back. A mountain rose so high its top disappeared into pink sky.

"That's Olympus Mons," said Rumble. "The biggest volcano anyone has ever found. It's about **thirteen and a half miles high** — almost three Mount Everests stacked up."

Theo's mouth fell open. "That's bigger than any world I've ever built."

"Earth squishes its mountains down flatter," said Rumble. "Mars just lets them grow and grow."

Juno tried to count its height on her fingers and gave up after ten. "Too big!"

Milo laughed. "I need way more LEGO bricks for this one."

"Time to head home," said Rumble softly, "but one more stop first."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Good Dirt
chapters.text:
They landed beside green, leafy fields at the foot of a quiet volcano. Farmers waved from rows of plants.

Milo looked puzzled. "Why would anyone live right next to a volcano?"

"Great question," said Rumble. "When ash falls, it breaks down into really good dirt — perfect for growing food."

Theo rubbed some dark soil between his fingers. "It just helps plants grow?"

"Just like that," said Rumble. "So people plant their fields close by, even knowing the mountain might rumble someday."

Juno patted the soil too. "It's warm and soft, like dinosaur dirt!"

Everybody laughed.

Milo thought about his own LEGO volcano, sitting quiet on his bedroom floor. "I think I understand volcanoes now," he said. "They're not scary. They're just Earth, breathing."

Rumble's glow pulsed warm and proud. "Well said, Milo."

"Time to go home," said Rumble. "I think three sleepy campers need their beds."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Bedroom Floor
chapters.text:
WHOOOSH! The glow swirled around them, and the bedroom floor rushed back up to meet their feet.

Milo blinked. He knelt right where he'd started, next to his little LEGO volcano. It still glowed, just a tiny bit, like a nightlight going to sleep.

"Goodbye, Rumble," whispered Juno, hugging her dinosaur tight.

"Not goodbye," crackled Rumble's voice, soft now, from deep inside the bricks. "See you next time something starts to rumble."

Theo set his tablet down, for once not minding that his game had paused. "That was better than any level I've ever played."

Milo picked up two new LEGO pieces. He snapped one into a wide, gentle shape, and one into a tall, pointy tower, just like the volcanoes they had seen.

"One of each," he said proudly, setting them side by side on the carpet.

Juno yawned a huge yawn and curled up beside her dinosaurs.

The little LEGO volcano gave one last happy HMMMMM, then its light faded to nothing, saving its rumbles for another night.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Theo. Keep rumbling, little volcanoes.

true_facts.text: A **volcano** is a hole in the ground where hot melted rock and gas squeeze out, like toothpaste from a tube.
Hot melted rock underground is called **magma**. Once it spills out on top, it's called **lava**.
The ground is made of giant moving pieces called **plates**, and many volcanoes grow where plates push, pull, or slide.
The **Ring of Fire** is a horseshoe shape around the Pacific Ocean where about three out of every four awake volcanoes live.
**Indonesia** has more awake volcanoes than any other country on Earth.
Hawaii's volcanoes grew over a **hotspot** — a patch of extra-hot rock deep underground, not at the edge of a plate.
**Kilauea** in Hawaii has been fizzing and popping almost nonstop for years and years.
**Mauna Loa** in Hawaii is the biggest awake volcano on the whole planet.
Some volcanoes are wide and gentle, like Hawaii's, and some are tall and steep, like a pointy hat.
In **1963**, a brand-new island named **Surtsey** popped up out of the sea near Iceland.
**Iceland** has lots of volcanoes because it sits where two giant plates pull apart.
**Olympus Mons** on Mars is the biggest volcano ever found — about thirteen and a half miles high, almost three Mount Everests stacked up.
Scientists use a tool called a **seismograph** to feel tiny wiggles in the ground, so they know if a volcano might wake up.

story.title: Juno and the Buzzy Meadow
story.subtitle: A tiny dinosaur, a big bee family, and one very sweet secret.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Spike Glows Green
chapters.text:
Juno sat on her rug. Her toy dinosaur, Spike, sat with her.

It was way past bedtime. Juno did not care.

Then Spike's eyes went GLOW-green. Spike started to buzz, just like a bee.

"Dinosaurs lived with bees," Spike said. "I even found one stuck in **amber** — that's hard golden rock, like candy turned to stone."

Spike puffed up big. ZOOOOM! The room got small, or maybe Juno got small.

They landed with a soft BONK on a giant yellow flower.

"Whoa," said Juno. "I am bee-sized!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Bee with Five Eyes
chapters.text:
"BZZZZZ!" A fuzzy bee landed right next to Juno.

"Hello!" said the bee. "I have five eyes!"

Juno blinked. "Five? I only have two!"

"Two big eyes see shapes and colors," said the bee. "Three tiny eyes sit on top of my head. They just feel light."

Juno counted on her fingers. "Two plus three is five!"

The bee buzzed happily. Her wings flapped two hundred times every second. That is why bees go BUZZZZZ.

"Come meet my sisters," said the bee.

Spike grinned. "Lead the way!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Busy, Busy Sisters
chapters.text:
At the hive, bees zoomed everywhere.

One swept the floor. One stood guard at the door. One zoomed off into the sky.

"Are they all different bees?" Juno asked.

"Nope!" said the bee. "We are all girls, and we take turns. Today I clean. Tomorrow I guard!"

Juno spotted some bigger, sleepy bees napping in the sun. "What do they do?"

"Not much," laughed the bee. "They're our brothers. Mostly us girls do the work!"

Juno giggled. "Just like my house."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Queen's Big Job
chapters.text:
Inside, a bee bigger than all the rest walked slowly, laying tiny white eggs.

"That's our queen," whispered the bee. "She's the busiest mom in the whole hive."

Juno started counting eggs. One, two, three... she lost count fast.

"She can lay two thousand eggs in one single day!" said the bee.

Juno's mouth popped open. "TWO THOUSAND?!"

"That's a LOT of brothers and sisters," said Spike.

The queen just kept laying, calm as could be.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Six Little Sides
chapters.text:
Juno looked at the walls. They were made of tiny rooms, each one with six flat sides.

"Why six sides?" Juno asked.

"Six sides fit together perfectly," said the bee. "No space gets wasted, so we can hold the most honey."

Juno traced one with her finger. "It's like a puzzle!"

"Want to help build one?" asked the bee.

Juno pressed warm, soft wax into a six-sided shape. CLICK! It fit right in.

"I built a bee room!" Juno cheered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Wiggle Dance
chapters.text:
A bee came zooming home, shaking her whole body in a wiggly little dance.

"What is she doing?" asked Juno.

"That's the waggle dance," said the bee. "She's telling everyone where the flowers are — which way, and how far."

Juno watched close, then copied the wiggle herself.

"This way!" Juno waggled toward the window. "Big flowers, not too far!"

The bees buzzed and followed Juno's wiggle.

They found a whole patch of yellow flowers!

"You did it, Juno!" said Spike.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Tiny Drops, Big Jar
chapters.text:
Juno watched bees land on flower after flower, sipping tiny drops of sweet juice from deep inside each one.

"One bee only makes a tiny bit of honey her whole life," said the bee. "Barely a drop!"

"Then how do you get a whole jar?" Juno asked.

"Lots and lots of bees, visiting millions of flowers," said the bee. "And while we visit, we help flowers grow into apples and blueberries too."

Juno helped carry one tiny drop home on a leaf. SPLOOSH! It plopped into the big honey jar.

"Every drop counts," said Juno, proud as could be.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Rug
chapters.text:
Spike puffed up again. ZOOOOM! The flowers shrank. The room grew big around Juno again.

She landed right back on her rug, exactly where she started.

On the carpet sat one tiny jar of honey, golden and warm.

"Bees made honey way before you were born," said Spike. "People even found old honey jars from long, long ago, and the honey was still good to eat!"

Juno smiled, sleepy now. "Just like you and your amber bee, Spike."

Spike's eyes glowed soft green, then faded to sleepy gray.

Juno hugged her little jar of honey and closed her eyes.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Buzz well.

true_facts.text: A bee family has one queen, lots of worker sisters, and fewer brother bees.
The queen bee can lay up to **two thousand eggs** in one single day.
Worker bees take turns doing all the jobs — cleaning, guarding, and finding flowers.
Bees have **five eyes** — two big ones for seeing, and three tiny ones for sensing light.
A bee's wings flap **two hundred times every second** — that's the buzzing sound!
Honeycomb rooms have **six sides**, so no space gets wasted.
Bees do a **waggle dance** to tell each other where the flowers are.
One bee makes only a **tiny drop** of honey in her whole life.
It takes bees visiting **millions of flowers** to make just one jar of honey.
Honey can stay **good to eat** for a very, very long time.
Bees lived alongside **dinosaurs**, a long, long time ago.
Bees help flowers grow into fruits like **apples and blueberries**.
