chapters.heading: Level 1: The Beeping Ball (1957)
chapters.text:
Theo was flat on his bedroom floor at 11:14 p.m., laptop propped on a pillow, building a rocket launcher for his new Roblox game. The launcher kept clipping through the floor of his map. Rude.

He nudged one more block into place and hit **Play Test**. The screen flickered black, then green, like a loading bar stuck halfway. Then a sound came out of the speakers that was not a notification ping and not his jump sound effect — just a steady, electric BEEP... BEEP... BEEP, over and over, like something very patient.

A blocky figure folded itself out of pixels where the Play button used to be: a visor, two glowing eyes, a body built out of squares. "NEW PLAYER DETECTED," it crackled. "I'm Commander Byte. I run on old code and older stories. Want to load a save file that actually happened?"

Theo sat up so fast he nearly knocked his laptop off the pillow. "Did you just — are you an NPC?"

"Close enough," said Byte. "Listen." The beeping got louder, and the room folded around it like a loading screen until Theo was standing — somehow, impossibly — in a dim room full of humming machines, a man in a lab coat hunched over a radio dial.

"That beep," Theo said slowly. "It's not random. It's steady, like a heartbeat. Is it... coming from the sky?"

"Good ears," said Byte. "On **October 4, 1957**, the Soviet Union launched something called **Sputnik 1** — a metal ball about the size of a beach ball, only about **58 centimeters wide**. It was the first thing people ever built that circled the whole planet, like a lap around a track, except the track was space. It didn't do much else. It just beeped. And that beep was so simple that regular people, with regular radios, could tune in and hear it for themselves."

Theo reached out and spun the dial himself, the way he'd line up a shot on frequency in a game. The beep sharpened, clean and clear. "It's basically the first-ever livestream," he said. "Everybody on Earth got the notification at once."

Byte's visor flickered — the NPC version of a grin. "PLAYER FOUND THE SIGNAL," he announced, and somewhere in the dim room, a dozen radios all over the world were doing exactly what Theo's had just done.

"Nobody had ever heard a sound from space before," Byte said. "Now a whole planet was listening at once — mostly to see who'd build the next cool thing."

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Dog Who Circled the World (1957–1958)
chapters.text:
Before Theo could ask another question, Commander Byte's visor flashed, and the humming room dissolved into cold tile and metal shelves. Somewhere close, a dog barked — short and sharp, then quiet, like a mic cutting out mid-stream.

"That's not a sound effect," Theo said, checking that his own hands were still there. "Where are we now?"

"One month later," said Byte. "**November 3, 1957**. The Soviets did it again, except this time they sent a passenger. A dog named **Laika** became the first living creature ever to circle the Earth."

Theo found a round window and looked in. A small dog with dark, patient eyes looked back at him. He didn't say anything for a second. "She's... actually famous, isn't she."

"People all over the world still know her name," Byte said quietly.

Theo turned away from the window, already thinking ahead. "Okay, but the Americans can't have just watched this happen. What did they do?"

"Good question," said Byte, and the scene reloaded into fluorescent light — a room full of men in short-sleeved shirts arguing over blueprints taped to a wall. "Sputnik scared the United States so badly that on **October 1, 1958**, they built a whole new agency just for space. They called it **NASA**."

"Like starting a brand-new server," Theo said, "because the old map wasn't cutting it."

"Pretty much exactly that. And their first real win came fast. On **January 31, 1958**, the US launched its own satellite, **Explorer 1**. It found something nobody even knew was up there — a wide, invisible ring wrapped around the Earth, made of tiny charged particles, like a sleeve of static the whole planet wears. Scientists now call it the **Van Allen radiation belt**, after the man whose instrument first noticed it."

Theo squinted at a looping readout on a nearby screen. A needle kept slamming to the top of the chart and resetting, over and over, like a counter that refused to behave. "Wait, is that supposed to do that? It's maxing out completely."

The scientist at the console — pencil behind one ear, tie loosened — froze and stared at the readout like Theo had just said something enormous.

"It is doing that," Byte confirmed. "And you just spotted exactly the clue the real scientists needed. The instrument wasn't broken. It was picking up way more radiation than anybody expected — which is how they found the belt in the first place."

"DISCOVERY UNLOCKED," Byte announced, and the fluorescent lights flickered like applause.

Theo grinned, already composing the patch notes in his head. "Two satellites in, and I've already helped find an invisible space ring nobody knew was there. Not bad for a Tuesday night."

chapters.heading: Level 3: The First Lap (1961)
chapters.text:
The lights snapped to a pad surrounded by scaffolding, and under Theo's boots the ground began to shake like bass through a subwoofer.

"Countdown's already running," Byte said. "You might want to cover your ears."

Theo didn't. He wanted to hear the whole thing: the rumble building into a roar, the rocket lifting off the pad in a wall of fire and smoke, climbing until it was just a bright dot. "Who's inside that?" he shouted over the noise.

"**Yuri Gagarin**," Byte called back, "a Soviet pilot. On **April 12, 1961**, he became the first human being ever to leave Earth. He rode a capsule called **Vostok 1** all the way around the planet once, in about **108 minutes**, and came back down."

Theo did the math out loud, the way he'd time a respawn. "That's less than two hours. He went around the *entire planet* in less time than it takes me to finish one build session."

"He also reportedly whistled a tune on the way up," Byte added. "Calm as anything."

Theo laughed, picturing it — a guy humming to himself while strapped to a controlled explosion. Then the scene rippled and reset, and they were standing on a different pad, smaller, with a stubby little capsule balanced on top.

"Three weeks later," Byte said, "on **May 5, 1961**, an American named **Alan Shepard** launched in a capsule called **Freedom 7**. He became the first American in space — though his flight didn't go all the way around. It arced up and came straight back down, like a kicked ball that never quite reaches the top corner of the goal."

Theo tilted his head. "So Gagarin did a full lap, and Shepard basically did a really, really high free kick."

"That's not a bad way to put it," Byte said. "Both of them mattered. One proved a human could survive going around. The other proved America could get a person up there too — even if the Soviets had the faster start."

Theo watched Shepard's capsule arc up and vanish, then splash down somewhere far off in blue. "So right now," he said slowly, "everybody on both sides is just racing to see who scores next."

"Exactly," said Byte. "And the biggest goal of the whole game hasn't even been called yet."

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Big Goal (1961–1963)
chapters.text:
The air changed before the scene did — a podium, a crowd, a man in a dark suit stepping up to a bank of microphones.

"Who's this?" Theo whispered.

"**President John F. Kennedy**," said Byte. "**May 25, 1961**. Watch."

Kennedy's voice rang out, steady and clear: a challenge to put a man on the Moon and bring him home safely, before the decade was out.

Theo's jaw actually dropped. "He just called that shot in front of everyone? Like, out loud, with no idea yet how to even do it?"

"That's exactly what he did," Byte said. "Like calling your shot before the whistle's even blown for the match. No backing out once you've said it on camera."

"That's either really brave or really risky," Theo said.

"Space tends to be both," said Byte.

The scene dissolved again, and this time they stood beside a launch tower under a bright sky, a different crowd buzzing with a different kind of excitement.

"**June 16, 1963**," Byte said. "Two years after Kennedy's speech. Watch who climbs in this time."

A woman in a flight suit walked to the capsule, helmet under one arm, and gave a short wave before she climbed inside.

"**Valentina Tereshkova**," Byte said. "She rode a capsule called **Vostok 6** and became the first woman ever to go to space."

Theo watched the rocket light up and climb. "Wait — she went up only two years after Gagarin? That's fast. Like, patch-update fast."

"The Soviets kept setting firsts," Byte agreed. "First satellite, first living creature in orbit, first man, now first woman. The Americans were still trying to catch up on the scoreboard."

Theo watched the dwindling rocket trail curve off into blue, already thinking about angles and arcs the way he thought about trajectories in his own builds. "So the goal's been called," he said. "Now somebody actually has to build the play that gets there."

"Somebody is," said Byte. "Several somebodies, actually. Want to meet one of them? He's not allowed to tell anyone his name."

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Secret Designer and the Spacewalk (1965)
chapters.text:
The next room was dim, paper everywhere, a single desk lamp pooling light over blueprints nobody outside the room was supposed to see.

"Why's this guy hiding in the dark?" Theo asked.

"Because he has to," said Byte. "This is **Sergei Korolev**, the chief designer behind the Soviet rocket program. He was the genius behind Sputnik, behind Gagarin's flight, behind almost everything you've seen so far — and his own country kept his name a complete secret. Most people didn't even learn who he really was until after he died, in **1966**."

Theo stared at the man hunched over his drawings, utterly unknown to the crowds cheering his rockets into the sky. "That's wild. He's basically the dev who built the whole game and never once showed up in the credits."

"Exactly like that," Byte said. "Meanwhile, on the other side, America's rocket genius was the opposite of secret." The scene shifted to a sunlit hangar, a tall man in shirtsleeves pointing at a rocket design taller than anything Theo had seen yet. "**Wernher von Braun** led the NASA team building a giant new rocket meant to reach the Moon itself. Everybody knew exactly who he was."

"One secret genius, one famous one," Theo said. "Same goal, totally different playstyle."

The scene shifted once more — stars, black silence, and a figure in a bulky white suit floating free outside a tiny spacecraft, tethered by a single thin cord.

"**March 18, 1965**," Byte said. "Soviet cosmonaut **Alexei Leonov**, floating completely outside his capsule, **Voskhod 2**. First human ever to leave a spacecraft and just... float there. About ten minutes, completely untethered from the ground, nothing below him but Earth."

Theo watched Leonov drift, turning slowly against a black backdrop sprinkled with stars, and felt his stomach flip a little — then settle, because the man on the tether was clearly fine, clearly working, clearly about to climb calmly back inside.

"That's either the best or the most terrifying thing I've ever seen," Theo said.

"He said it was beautiful," Byte said. "Silent, and beautiful, and over too soon."

Theo watched Leonov swing himself back through the hatch, safe, and let out a breath he hadn't realized he was holding. "Okay. Add 'float in space on a string' to my list of things I definitely want to try in a game first."

chapters.heading: Level 6: Earthrise (December 1968)
chapters.text:
The next load screen didn't show a launch pad at all. It showed nothing — just black, and a tiny round window, and Theo's own breathing suddenly loud in his ears.

"Where's the ground?" he asked.

"There isn't one," Byte said. "Not under you, anyway. **December 1968**. You're riding along with the crew of **Apollo 8** — the first humans ever to leave Earth's orbit entirely and circle the Moon."

Theo pressed close to the window. Gray, cratered ground slid by below, close enough to touch, strange and silent.

Then the capsule rolled, and over the gray horizon, something came up that made Theo forget to say anything at all: a small, blue, impossibly bright marble, rising against the blackness like a sunrise, except it was the whole Earth.

"Whoa," he finally managed.

"That's **Earthrise**," Byte said quietly. "One of the astronauts, **William Anders**, grabbed a camera and took the photo right as it happened. Nobody had planned it. He just saw it and knew."

Theo stared at the little blue marble, every single person he'd ever met somewhere on its surface, all of it fitting behind his own thumb if he held it up to the window. "That's everyone," he said slowly. "That's literally everyone, in one picture."

"It changed how a lot of people thought about home," Byte said. "Funny thing about a space race — sometimes the best shot isn't of where you're going. It's of where you started."

Theo kept his hand pressed to the glass a moment longer than he needed to. Then he grinned, because he'd just thought of something. "I'm putting a sky-box like that in my game. Nobody's gonna believe it's real until I tell them it actually happened."

"They never do," said Byte. "That's the best part of this whole save file."

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Giant Leap (July 1969)
chapters.text:
The ground came back hard and sudden — gray dust, black sky at noon, a rocket standing behind them so tall Theo had to lean all the way back to see the top of it.

"That thing is enormous," he said.

"**Saturn V**," Byte said. "**363 feet tall** — taller than the Statue of Liberty. It's what got the **Apollo 11** crew all the way here."

Theo turned a slow circle, taking in the dust, the stillness, the sky with no blue in it anywhere. "Wait. Here, here? Like — we're actually—"

"**July 20, 1969**," Byte said. "Watch the ladder."

A bulky white boot came down out of a hatch above them, found a rung, then another, and finally touched the gray dust below with a small, silent puff.

"**Neil Armstrong**," Byte said. "First human being to ever stand on the Moon. He called it one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind."

Theo stood frozen, watching footprints appear in dust that had never once been disturbed in the entire history of the planet. A second astronaut climbed down to join the first.

"That's **Buzz Aldrin**," Byte said. "He came down to join Armstrong. A third astronaut, **Michael Collins**, stayed up above the whole time, flying the command module **Columbia** in a big slow loop, completely alone, waiting for the other two to come back up."

Theo looked up at the black sky, trying to spot a dot that might be Collins circling somewhere above them, patient and solo. "That seems like a rough job. Everyone remembers the two guys who got out and walked. Nobody remembers the guy flying laps upstairs."

"Somebody has to fly the getaway car," Byte said. "Without him, neither of those boots gets home."

Theo crouched and pressed his own fingers into the dust beside one of the fresh footprints, just to feel it. It was soft, and cold, and completely real.

"For the record," Byte added, "this wasn't the only trip. Between **1969 and 1972**, twelve different American astronauts walked on the Moon across six separate landings. Armstrong and Aldrin just got here first."

Theo stood back up, grinning at the footprints like they were his own high score. "First place on the leaderboard," he said. "But not the only run that counted."

chapters.heading: Level 8: The Fix and the Handshake (1970–1975)
chapters.text:
The gray dust vanished into the cramped metal of a capsule, warning lights blinking red across a panel, three astronauts strapped in tight, voices clipped and careful.

"What happened here?" Theo asked, feeling the tension in the room before he understood it.

"**1970**,** Apollo 13**," Byte said. "An oxygen tank exploded on the way to the Moon. The mission couldn't land anymore — the whole plan broke."

Theo's stomach tightened. "Are they okay?"

"Watch," said Byte, calm. Down on a different screen, rows of engineers in short-sleeved shirts bent over a table scattered with random spare parts — hoses, bags, cardboard, tape — building something that looked nothing like a spaceship part and everything like a school project.

"They had to invent a fix using only what the astronauts already had on board," Byte said. "No new parts, no do-overs. Just problem-solving, fast, under pressure."

Theo watched the engineers test their strange cardboard contraption, then nod, then radio instructions up to the capsule. The warning lights steadied. The voices on the radio, which had been tight and quiet, slowly relaxed.

"They got the crew home safely," Byte said. "All three of them. Sometimes the best move in the whole game is admitting the plan broke, and building a new one out of whatever's left in your inventory."

Theo let out a long breath. "Okay. That's genuinely the best clutch save I've ever heard of."

The scene dissolved one final time, gentler now — a wide black sky, two spacecraft drifting slowly toward each other, nose to nose, like two players finally meeting at center field.

"**July 17, 1975**," Byte said. "An American spacecraft and a Soviet spacecraft **docked together** in orbit — locked their hatches together like puzzle pieces clicking into place. The crews floated through and shook hands, right there above the Earth."

Theo watched the handshake happen in complete silence, no gravity, no sound at all, just two hands meeting. "So after all that racing," he said slowly, "it ends with everybody just... saying good game?"

"Something like that," Byte said. "Eighteen years, start to finish. Beeping ball to handshake in orbit."

The room folded in on itself one last time, green light narrowing back down to a familiar glow — and Theo was on his bedroom floor again, laptop warm under his hands, the Play Test screen still open exactly where he'd left it.

On the carpet beside him sat something that hadn't been there before: a small, scuffed metal ball, about the size of a beach ball in miniature, with four thin antennae curling off it like legs. It beeped once, softly, and went quiet.

Theo picked it up carefully and set it on his desk, right next to his keyboard, where he'd see it first thing tomorrow.

"Same time next save file?" Byte's voice crackled, already fading.

"Count on it," Theo said.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a rocket launcher to finally get right — and a whole new level in mind.

story.title: Maya and the Porthole Boat
story.subtitle: A bedtime voyage to the great ship Titanic.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Shipyard in Belfast (1909)
chapters.text:
Maya was drawing boats on her bedroom floor, way past bedtime. Her swimming medal hung on the lamp, glowing gold.

On her windowsill sat her favorite wooden toy boat. Tonight its little round porthole window began to glow, green and gold, like water lit by sun.

Maya touched it. **WHOOOOSH!** Salty wind filled her room. A tiny sailor popped out, covered in little sea shells, with a seashell hat tilted sideways.

"Permission to come aboard, Maya?" he said. "I'm First Mate Barnacle. Smooth sailing tonight — we're going way back, to **1909**."

They landed on a loud, clanging shipyard in **Belfast, Ireland**. Workers were laying down a huge metal beam.

"That's the **keel**," said Barnacle. "It's the long backbone of the ship. Everything else gets built on top of it."

Maya traced the keel's shape in her sketchbook, matching its long curve exactly. "It's going to be enormous," she said.

"You're right," said Barnacle. "A company called **Harland & Wolff** is building her, for the **White Star Line**. She'll be called **Titanic**."

Maya grinned and drew a tiny flag on top of her sketch. The workers cheered, and somehow, so did she.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Launch (1911)
chapters.text:
A horn blared, long and low. Maya jumped. "What's happening?"

"Fast forward," said Barnacle, spinning his little wheel. "It's **1911** now. Watch this."

The huge ship, finished at last, slid down into the water. **SPLOOSH!** Waves rolled out in rings, rocking tiny boats nearby.

Maya held up her sketchbook next to the ship to compare sizes. Her whole page looked tiny. "She's so long!"

"**882 feet**," said Barnacle. "Longer than two soccer fields. The biggest ship anyone had ever built."

Maya spotted two more ships being built nearby, shaped just the same. "Are those her sisters?"

"Good eye," said Barnacle. "Titanic had two: **Olympic** and **Britannic**. Triplets, almost."

Maya waved at the workers cheering on the dock, and they waved back like old friends.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Southampton Morning (10 April 1912)
chapters.text:
Crowds roared. Seagulls shrieked. A band played somewhere down the dock.

"**10 April 1912**," said Barnacle. "Titanic's very first trip. Everyone's heading to New York City."

Maya counted the smokestacks rising above the deck. "One, two, three, four!"

"Sharp counting," said Barnacle, "but only three of those puff real smoke. The fourth one's just there to look grand."

Maya giggled. "A fake chimney? That's sneaky."

Below deck, Maya found a wall with thick metal doors. "What are these for?"

"Those close off little rooms called **compartments**," Barnacle explained. "If water ever got in one, the doors could shut, and the rest of the ship would stay dry. People said that made her almost impossible to sink."

Maya traced the doors in her sketchbook, drawing each one shut tight, like a puzzle she wanted to solve.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: A Bump in the Night (14 April 1912)
chapters.text:
The air turned icy. Maya pulled her sleeves down over her hands.

"**14 April 1912**," whispered Barnacle. "Nighttime, out in the middle of the ocean."

Then Maya saw it — a pale, glowing shape ahead in the dark water. "Barnacle, look! Is that ice?"

"An iceberg," he said. "Good catch, Maya."

A bell clanged. The ship turned, but too slowly. **CRUNCH.** A shiver ran along the hull.

Maya grabbed Barnacle's little shell hat to steady herself. "Are we okay?"

"We're just watching, safe and sound," said Barnacle gently. "But down there, water was leaking into some of those compartments. More than the doors could hold back."

Maya nodded slowly, hugging her sketchbook. "Then people needed help."

"They did," said Barnacle. "And help was already on its way."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Calling for Help
chapters.text:
Tap-tap-tap-tap. A strange clicking noise echoed from a little room at the top of the ship.

Maya peeked inside. Two men sat hunched over a buzzing machine. "What's that sound?"

"That's **wireless**,” said Barnacle. “No telephone wires — just signals zapping through the air. Those are **Jack Phillips** and **Harold Bride**, calling other ships for help."

Maya listened to the pattern. "It sounds like a song."

"It's a code," said Barnacle. "Old sailors used three letters, **CQD**. But that night they also tried a brand-new one — **SOS**. Easier to tap, easier to remember."

Far off on deck, Maya heard music too — violins, soft and steady. "Someone's playing in the cold?"

"People say the band kept playing to help everyone feel calm," said Barnacle. "Nobody wrote down every tune for certain, but it's a lovely story, and it might be true."

Maya hummed along, quietly, so the music wouldn't feel so alone.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Boats on the Water
chapters.text:
Maya climbed to the deck and gasped. Little wooden lifeboats were being lowered, creaking, into the black water.

"There aren't very many," Maya said, counting worriedly.

"You're right," said Barnacle. "Those boats could only hold about **1,178** people — not everyone aboard. It was a big lesson Titanic taught the whole world."

Maya spotted a woman rowing hard, shouting cheerful instructions to the people around her. "Who's that?"

"**Molly Brown**," said Barnacle. "She grabbed an oar and rowed like a champion. People later called her 'the Unsinkable Molly Brown.'"

Maya noticed two fluffy little dogs tucked into a passenger's coat, riding safely in a boat. She smiled and pointed instead of reaching to pet them, just watching them snuggle warm.

Far off, a ship's light appeared on the horizon. "That's the **Carpathia**," said Barnacle. "She raced through the night and picked up everyone from the lifeboats the next morning. And **Captain Edward Smith** stayed until the very end, making sure others got to safety first."

Maya let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding. "They made it."

"Lots of them did," said Barnacle, "because people were brave."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Found in the Deep (1985)
chapters.text:
The scene shimmered, and suddenly the water turned dark and still.

"**1985** now," said Barnacle. "Deep, deep down — about **12,500 feet**, further than any sunlight reaches."

A little robot submarine floated past with bright lights, taking pictures. "Who's driving that?" Maya asked.

"**Robert Ballard** and his team," said Barnacle. "They searched for years and finally found the wreck, split into two big pieces on the seafloor, off the coast of **Newfoundland, Canada**."

Maya drew the broken ship carefully, shading the dark water around it. "It still looks like a ship, even broken."

"People have found dinner plates, shoes, all sorts of things down there," said Barnacle. "Now they sit safely in museums, so everyone can remember."

"Like a museum shaped like the ship itself?" Maya guessed.

"Exactly — **Titanic Belfast**, built in **2012**, right where she was first made," said Barnacle, impressed. "And there's even a famous movie about her, from **1997**."

Maya closed her sketchbook gently, like tucking the ship in for the night.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Windowsill
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH!** The salty wind swirled backward, and Maya landed softly on her bedroom floor.

Her toy boat sat on the windowsill again, porthole glowing faintly, then fading to plain wood.

First Mate Barnacle tipped his shell hat. "Smooth sailing tonight, Maya. You spotted the iceberg, you counted the smokestacks, and you never once let go of your sketchbook."

Maya looked down at her drawings — the keel, the compartments, Molly Brown rowing, the little robot submarine in the dark. A whole ship's story, in her own hand.

"Will we sail again?" she asked, yawning.

"Always," said Barnacle, and with a tiny wave, he popped back inside the porthole.

Maya tucked her sketchbook under her pillow and climbed into bed, her swimming medal glowing softly on the lamp above her.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. Sail well.

story.title: Ivy and the Rainbow Raindrop
story.subtitle: A puddle, a paintbrush, and a sky full of color

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Puddle
chapters.text:
Ivy sat on her bedroom floor. She painted a big blue puddle. Rain tapped the window. Tap, tap, tap.

Then her paint water began to glow. It sparkled like tiny stars. A small round light popped up. It had a shiny raindrop shape.

"Hello, Ivy!" it said. "I'm Pip. I'm a raindrop friend. Want to see how rainbows are made?"

Ivy's eyes went wide. "Yes!" she said. She grabbed her paintbrush like a magic wand. WHOOSH! The puddle pulled them both right outside, into the rain.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Sun and Rain, Together
chapters.text:
Rain tapped Ivy's nose. Pat, pat, pat.

Pip floated close, round and shiny as a dewdrop. "Rainbows need two things," he said. "Sun. And rain. Both at the very same time."

Ivy looked up. The clouds were still gray and heavy. No sun yet, not even a peek.

"We wait," said Pip. "Just a little bit. Rainbows are patient like that."

Ivy sat down in a puddle to wait. Splash! Cool water tickled her toes.

Then a tiny gold light poked through a crack in the clouds. Ivy gasped. "The sun! It's peeking out!"

Pip clapped his tiny hands. SPLASH! Raindrops jumped off his shiny hat. "Now we have both," he said. "Sun and rain, together. That means rainbow time is coming!"

"SUN AND RAIN!" Ivy cheered, waving her paintbrush like a wand.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Turn Around, Ivy!
chapters.text:
Pip tugged gently on Ivy's sleeve. "Which way are you facing?" he asked.

Ivy pointed toward a big puddle. "Toward the rain," she said proudly.

Pip shook his head, droplets sliding off his chin. "Try this instead. Put the sun behind you. Put the rain in front."

Ivy turned around slowly, one careful step at a time. Warm sunshine landed on her back. Cool rain misted her face.

Nothing happened yet. Ivy frowned and tapped her foot.

"Look up," Pip whispered.

Ivy tipped her head back and looked up. A bright, curved stripe of color stretched clear across the sky!

"THERE IT IS!" Ivy shouted, pointing with her paintbrush like she was painting the sky herself.

Pip grinned so wide his whole round body wobbled. "Sun behind, rain in front. That little trick works every single time."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Inside One Tiny Drop
chapters.text:
Ivy wanted to see inside a raindrop. "Can we go in?" she asked, bouncing on her toes.

Pip nodded and waved one tiny hand. Ivy shrank down, tiny as a speck of paint. WHOOSH! Together they zoomed into one shiny, round raindrop.

Sunlight came streaming through, like a sunbeam sneaking through a window.

"Watch closely," said Pip. "The light bends a little when it comes in."

The beam tilted sideways, just like Pip said.

"Now it bounces off the back wall," Pip explained.

The light bounced, like a ball off a wall. BONK!

"Then it bends again on the way out," said Pip, "and that's when it splits into colors!"

Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple burst out the other side, bright as new paint.

Ivy clapped both hands. "Paint colors! Those are my paint colors, Pip!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Color Line-Up
chapters.text:
Back outside, Ivy stared up at the rainbow, tracing its curve with one finger. "Which color goes first?" she asked.

Pip smiled, bobbing gently beside her. "You tell me. You're the painter, Ivy."

Ivy pointed at the very top stripe. "Red," she said. "Like my apple painting on the fridge."

"Then orange," she added, "like a puddle full of carrots."

"Yellow, green, blue," Ivy sang out, bouncing from foot to foot.

"And last of all," she said, grinning, "purple. Like my pajamas!"

Pip twirled happily in the air, leaving little sparkles behind. "You just painted the whole sky, Ivy, color by color."

Ivy giggled and dipped her paintbrush toward the rainbow, pretending to touch each glowing stripe, one by one.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Back to the Puddle
chapters.text:
The rain slowed, then stopped. The rainbow began to soften and fade.

"Time to go home," Pip said gently, floating close.

The puddle on Ivy's painting began to glow once more. WHOOSH! Ivy landed back on her bedroom floor, paintbrush still tucked safely in her hand.

On her paper, a brand-new picture had appeared, right where her blue puddle used to be: a little rainbow, painted in perfect stripes.

Pip's voice echoed softly, fading like a lullaby. "Sun behind you, rain in front. Remember the trick, Ivy."

Ivy yawned a big, sleepy yawn. She hugged her paintbrush close. "I will, Pip. Goodnight."

She climbed into bed and pulled up her blanket, dreaming of colors dripping like fresh, wet paint.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ivy. Paint bright, dream bright.

true_facts.text: A rainbow needs both sun and rain happening at the same time.
Rainbows often show up right after it rains, when the sun starts peeking out.
To see a rainbow, you put the sun behind you and the rain in front of you.
That 'sun behind, rain in front' trick works every time.
Sunlight bends a little bit when it goes into a raindrop.
Inside the raindrop, the light bounces off the back, like a ball off a wall.
The light bends again on its way out of the drop.
That bending and bouncing is what splits sunlight into all the rainbow colors.
Rainbow colors line up in order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple.

story.title: Leo and the Sleepy Express
story.subtitle: A nighttime train ride into why we sleep

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Owl Light Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Leo lined up his red train cars one more time. His room was almost dark, and the dark felt big.

On the shelf, Ollie the Owl nightlight blinked once. Blink. Blink.

"Psst, Leo," Ollie whispered. "Want to see why everybody sleeps?"

Leo sat up fast. "Owls don't talk!"

"This one does," said Ollie, and his chest glowed warm and gold.

A tiny train chugged right out of the glow. **CHUFF. CHUFF.** Its doors popped open.

Leo hopped inside before he could even wonder how.

"All aboard the Sleepy Express," said Ollie, swooping to the front. "First stop, **1953**."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Blinking Eyes (1953)
chapters.text:
The train stopped beside a cozy bed. A boy slept there, snug under his blanket.

Leo leaned close. "Ollie, look! His eyes are wiggling!"

Under the boy's eyelids, his eyes flicked side to side, fast as a Ping-Pong ball.

A man in a white coat leaned in too. "I see it," he said. "I'm **Eugene Aserinsky**. I'm watching eyes move while someone dreams."

His teacher, **Nathaniel Kleitman**, studied sleep for many years too, writing down everything they learned.

"So that's dream sleep!" said Leo.

"That's right," said Ollie. "In **1953**, Eugene found this wiggly, dreamy kind of sleep. You spotted it just like he did."

Leo puffed up proud as a steam engine.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Up the Dreamy Hill
chapters.text:
The tracks curved into a big loop. Up, down. Up, down.

"Whoa, we keep going in circles!" said Leo.

"Good eye," said Ollie. "Sleep loops too. Each loop is about ninety minutes, a little longer than your favorite movie."

Down in the valley, the train rolled slow and quiet. That's **quiet sleep**, resting and still.

Up on the hill, the train jiggled and bounced. That's **dream sleep**, when your brain gets busy again.

Leo tried to wiggle his toes on the hill part. They wouldn't budge!

"Your body goes soft and still in dream sleep," said Ollie, "so you don't act out your dreams and tumble out of bed."

Leo giggled. "Lucky feet."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Baby Owlet Car
chapters.text:
The next stop smelled like warm feathers. Soft coos came from a round nest-car.

Leo peeked in. Tiny owlets were curled up, fast asleep, every single one.

"They sleep a LOT," Leo whispered.

"Newborn babies do too," said Ollie. "Fourteen to seventeen hours a day, in little naps."

Leo counted on his fingers. "That's almost the whole day!"

"Mostly dream sleep, too," said Ollie, "so their brains can grow busy and strong."

One owlet yawned so wide it tipped backward. Leo caught it gently and tucked it back in.

"Sleep tight, little one," he whispered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Sleepy Animal Station
chapters.text:
Three round windows glowed on the platform: one blue, one spotty, one dark and furry.

"Pick a window," said Ollie.

Leo tapped the blue one first. A dolphin swam by with one eye open.

"Dolphins sleep with half their brain at a time," said Ollie. "One eye stays open to watch for danger and keep swimming."

Leo tapped the spotty window next. A giraffe stood very still, eyes half shut.

"Giraffes barely nap," said Ollie. "Sometimes less than two hours a day, in little standing snoozes."

Leo tapped the furry window last. A tiny bat hung upside down, snoring softly.

"Bats sleep up to twenty hours," said Ollie. "That's almost the whole day and night!"

"ONE EYE OPEN!" Leo shouted, waving at the dolphin window.

Ollie laughed. "Everybody sleeps differently. Even animals."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Remembering Tracks
chapters.text:
The tracks split into dozens of tiny tracks, like a puzzle.

"Why do we even need sleep?" Leo asked.

"Sleep sorts your day," said Ollie, "like putting train cars on the right tracks. Things you practiced today get tucked into memory, so you remember them tomorrow."

"Like my choo-choo noises?" Leo grinned.

"Exactly like that," said Ollie. "And deep quiet sleep helps your body grow, a little more every night."

Leo stood up tall. "I grew a whole inch since my birthday!"

Ollie added, "People spend about a third of their whole life asleep!"

Leo's eyes went wide. "That's SO much sleep."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Back to the Nightlight
chapters.text:
The tiny train chugged back toward the glow it came from.

**CHUFF. CHUFF.** The doors popped open onto Leo's own carpet.

His red train cars sat right where he'd left them.

On the shelf, Ollie the Owl blinked once, warm and gold, just a nightlight again.

But on the carpet sat one small golden feather that hadn't been there before.

Leo picked it up and tucked it under his pillow.

He lay back down, eyes getting heavy, dream sleep already waiting.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Leo. Choo choo, sleep tight.

true_facts.text: In **1953**, **Eugene Aserinsky** watched a sleeping boy's eyes wiggle and found dream sleep.
His teacher, **Nathaniel Kleitman**, studied sleep for many years too.
A night of sleep goes in loops about **ninety minutes** long.
In dream sleep your brain gets busy, but your body stays soft and still.
Newborn babies sleep about **fourteen to seventeen hours** a day, in little naps.
**Dolphins** sleep with only half their brain at a time, keeping one eye open.
**Giraffes** barely nap, sometimes less than two hours a day.
Some little **bats** sleep up to twenty hours a day.
Sleep helps sort the day's memories, so you remember what you practiced.
Deep, quiet sleep helps your body grow a little more every night.
People spend about a third of their whole life asleep.

story.title: Rosa and Isla and the Sticky Climbing Club
story.subtitle: A bedtime trip to meet the wall-climbers of the world.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Dot Finds a Gecko
chapters.text:
Rosa sat on her bedroom rug. She held her favorite toy. A little red ladybird with black spots.

"One, two, three, four," she counted its spots.

Isla sat close by. She was reading about rock climbing. She loved big rocks and tiny footholds.

Then the ladybird toy blinked. Its spots glowed bright red! "Hello," it said.

Rosa dropped it in surprise. It buzzed. Little wings of light popped out. It hovered right in front of them.

"I'm Dot," said the ladybird. "Want to see how animals climb walls?"

"YES!" said Isla and Rosa together.

They shrank down, tiny as Dot. **WHOOOOSH!** Out the window they zoomed.

They landed on a cool window pane. Above them hung a small lizard, upside down, not falling at all.

"That's a **gecko**," said Dot.

"How does he not fall?" asked Rosa.

Dot grinned. "His feet have millions of tiny hairs, too small to see."

Isla leaned close. "His toes peel off like sticky tape!"

"Smart girl," said Dot. "It's not glue. He just peels each toe up, one at a time, and lifts off clean."

Rosa tried peeling her own fingers off the glass. She got stuck for a giggly second, then popped free.

"IT'S NOT GLUE!" she shouted.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Buzzy Window
chapters.text:
Dot zoomed to a different window. A fat black fly sat on the glass.

It walked up, down, sideways. It never once fell off.

"How does he do that?" asked Isla.

Dot landed beside the fly. "Look at his tiny feet," she said.

Rosa peered close. Tiny round pads sat under each foot.

"Each pad makes a tiny wet drop," said Dot. "The drop sticks like glue. Just for a second."

Isla pressed her own finger to the glass. She pulled it back. "Sticky!" she said. "Like a tiny kiss of water."

"Exactly," said Dot. "He lifts his foot, and the drop lets go."

Rosa tried it too. She dabbed her finger on the glass, then peeled it off. **POP!**

"My finger is a fly foot!" she giggled.

Isla grinned. "Science is everywhere," she said. "Even on buzzy windows."

Dot flashed her red spots. "Ready for the next one?"

"YES!" said both girls.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Eight Legs, Many Hairs
chapters.text:
Next stop: a corner web, sparkly with dew.

A spider sat there, still as a stone.

"One, two, three, four..." Rosa counted its legs. She got to eight.

"Eight legs!" she cheered.

Isla looked closer. "Its feet look fuzzy," she said. "Like tiny brushes."

"Good eye," said Dot. "Spiders have thousands of tiny hairs on their feet. Thinner than Rosa's own hair."

"Are they like gecko hairs?" asked Isla.

"Just like them," said Dot. "That is why spiders can climb smooth glass too."

Rosa watched the spider creep up the window, not slipping once.

"Can we see the hairs even closer?" Isla asked.

Dot winked. "Hold on tight."

**ZOOOOM!** The world got bigger. Tiny hairs covered the spider's feet like a soft, furry carpet.

"Whoa," whispered Isla. "It's like a thousand tiny fingers."

Rosa reached toward the web, then stopped herself.

"We just look," she said. "No touching the spider's home."

"Smart girl," said Dot.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Tool-Swapping Ants
chapters.text:
They landed near a rough brick wall. Ants marched straight up it.

Then an ant crossed onto a smooth window. It slowed down, then kept right on climbing.

"How did it do that?" asked Rosa.

Isla watched closely. "Maybe it uses different feet for different walls," she guessed.

Dot clapped her tiny wings. "Exactly right! Ants have sharp little claws for rough walls, and sticky pads for smooth ones. They swap, depending on the wall."

"Like changing shoes!" said Isla. "I use grippy shoes for rock, and different ones for smooth walls at the climbing gym."

"Just like that," said Dot.

Rosa watched a cockroach do the same trick on a nearby pipe.

"They're twins!" she said, pointing between the ant and the cockroach.

"Close enough," laughed Dot. "Both switch their tools to match the wall."

Isla nodded. "I'm going to try that at the gym," she said. "Smart shoes for every rock."

Dot's spots glowed brighter. "Then you'll climb like an ant," she said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Goat Shoes on a Cliff
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH!** Dot carried them high, over a rocky mountain.

A goat stood on a cliff edge, barely wider than its own hooves.

"Won't it fall?" asked Rosa, eyes wide.

"Watch its feet," said Dot.

Isla leaned in. "The edge looks hard," she said, "but the middle looks soft and squishy."

"You're right again," said Dot. "A hard rim grips the rock. A soft, squishy middle molds around every bump."

"Like my climbing shoes!" said Isla. "Hard edges, soft rubber underneath."

The goat hopped calmly to another ledge, never slipping once.

Rosa let out a breath. "Phew. It's okay," she said. "Its feet are just really good at this."

"Mountain goats do this every single day," said Dot. "No big deal to them."

Isla grinned. "I want goat shoes for climbing," she said.

"Maybe someday," said Dot, "people will make shoes just like that."

Rosa clapped. "Goat shoes! Goat shoes!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Squirrel Secrets in the Bark
chapters.text:
Down they zoomed, to a tall, bumpy tree.

A squirrel ran straight up the trunk, fast as a blink.

"How does it grip?" asked Rosa, patting her toy ladybird's spots.

Isla squinted at the bark. "I don't see anything to hold onto," she said.

"Look closer," said Dot. **ZOOOOM!** The bark grew huge before their eyes.

Tiny cracks and bumps appeared, too small to see before.

"There they are!" said Isla. "Tiny cracks, everywhere!"

"The squirrel's claws are sharp and curved," said Dot. "They hook into cracks too small for us to notice."

Rosa touched the bark gently with one finger. "Bumpy," she said. "Like my ladybird's back."

"Just like that," said Dot, smiling.

The squirrel paused at the top and flicked its tail, as if waving.

Rosa waved back. "Bye, squirrel!"

Isla laughed. "I think it likes you."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Hexagon Toes
chapters.text:
Rain pattered on wide green leaves. A small frog sat on one, upside down.

"It's not even sliding," said Isla, "and the leaf is wet!"

Dot landed close. "Tree frogs have special toe pads," she said. "Covered in sticky slime, with tiny little shapes on them."

Rosa peeked at the frog's toes. "What shapes?"

"Hexagons," said Dot. "A hexagon is a shape with six sides, like a tiny honeycomb."

Isla counted the sides on one toe pad. "One, two, three... six! You're right."

The frog blinked, then hopped to another leaf, landing with a soft **SPLAT**, sticking fast.

Rosa reached a finger toward it, then pulled back. "We just watch," she said, remembering the spider.

"Good girl," said Dot. "Frogs like to be watched, not touched."

Isla smiled. "Science rule number one," she said. "Hands off, eyes on."

Dot's spots flickered happily. "Now, one more stop," she said. "A very special one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Sticky Gloves and Home Again
chapters.text:
Dot flew them to a bright room full of screens and tiny lizard pictures.

A kind scientist smiled at them — a person who studies how things work.

"This is where people study gecko feet," said Dot.

Isla's eyes went wide. "Can people climb like geckos too?"

"Some have tried," said Dot. "In **2014**, scientists made sticky paddles. A man used them to climb straight up a glass wall."

"No glue, no ropes?" asked Isla.

"Just sticky paddles," said Dot, "copying gecko toes."

Isla punched the air. "I want gecko gloves for climbing!"

Rosa yawned a big yawn. "I want my bed," she said.

Dot giggled. "Time to go home, little ladybird."

**WHOOOOSH!** The world spun, and they landed back on Rosa's soft rug.

The toy ladybird sat still again. But now, one of its spots was shaped like a tiny hexagon.

"Look!" whispered Rosa, pointing at the new spot.

Isla smiled. "A little souvenir," she said. "From our sticky adventure."

Dot's glow dimmed to a soft shine. "Climb well," she whispered, "both of you."

Rosa hugged the ladybird close and climbed into bed.

Isla tucked her blanket in, grinning at the ceiling. "Tomorrow," she whispered, "I'm trying goat shoes at the climbing gym."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Rosa. Goodnight, Isla. Climb well.

true_facts.text: Geckos can run up glass and walk on ceilings because their toes have millions of tiny hairs, too small to see.
A gecko's sticky feet aren't glue — it peels each toe off, one at a time, to let go clean.
Flies have tiny pads on their feet that make a tiny wet drop, sticking like glue for just a second.
Spiders have thousands of tiny hairs on their feet, like gecko hairs, which is why they can climb smooth glass.
Ants and cockroaches use sharp claws on rough walls and sticky pads on smooth ones, swapping tools to match the wall.
Mountain goats have hooves with a hard edge and a soft, squishy middle that molds around bumps on the rock.
Squirrels use sharp, curved claws that hook into tiny cracks in bark, too small for us to see.
Tree frogs have sticky, slime-covered toe pads with tiny six-sided hexagon shapes that help them stick to wet leaves.
Scientists study gecko and insect feet to invent sticky gloves and shoes that help people climb too.

story.title: Milo, Juno and the Dinosaur That Clicked
story.subtitle: A giant, roaring trip back 230 million years — with a LEGO brick as the ticket.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Brick Wakes Up
chapters.text:
The tower from last night was still standing. Its top brick still held tight.

Milo lay on the rug. He lined up his LEGO shark next to the tower.

Juno flopped down beside him, hugging a plastic dinosaur.

"Dinosaurs are way older than sharks," Juno said.

"Nuh-uh," said Milo. Then the top brick began to glow red.

It pulsed. It clicked. **CLICK. CLICK. CLICK.**

"It's doing the thing again!" Milo whispered.

The brick lifted off the tower and hung in the air, humming.

"When do you want to go?" it asked, in a small clicky voice.

"Dinosaur times!" Juno shouted. "The very first one!"

The brick glowed brighter. "Good guess. Dinosaurs started about **230 million years ago**. That is a lot of birthdays."

"WHOOOOSH!" yelled the brick.

The bedroom spun into green and gold. Ferns brushed their knees. Hot air smelled like dirt and rain.

Something small and quick darted past their feet.

"That's a dinosaur!" Juno said. "One of the first ones!"

"How do you know what a dinosaur even means?" Milo asked.

The brick clicked happily. "Long ago, a scientist named it. **Dinosaur** means 'terrible lizard.' He just thought they looked fierce."

Juno puffed out her chest and stomped like a terrible lizard.

Milo laughed so hard he fell in the ferns.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Three-Horned Friend
chapters.text:
Something stomped behind the ferns. **THUD. THUD. THUD.**

Milo froze. Juno did not.

She peeked around a big leaf. "It's not scary," she said. "Look at its face!"

A huge dinosaur stepped out. It had three horns on its head. A big bony collar circled its neck, like a shield made of bone.

"That shield is called a **frill**," said the brick. "It helps protect the neck."

Milo looked closer. "Wait. I can count the horns!"

"One, two, three!" Juno shouted, pointing at each.

"You found it," said the brick, clicking happily. "This is Triceratops. Three horns, one frill."

The big dinosaur chomped some ferns, calm as a cow in a field.

Juno waved at it, careful to stay back. "We just look," she said. "No touching."

"Smart rule," said the brick. "Even Milo's sharks get that same rule at the zoo."

Milo grinned. "Three horns is still less cool than a shark fin. But okay, pretty cool."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Teeth Like Daggers
chapters.text:
A giant shadow slid across the ferns. Something huge walked by, teeth flashing like knives.

Milo gasped. "Are those real teeth?"

"That is Tyrannosaurus rex," said the brick. "T. rex, for short."

Milo held up two fingers, close together. "My toy shark tooth is only this big."

"T. rex teeth were way bigger," said the brick. "Up to **twelve inches long**. That's almost as long as a ruler and a half!"

Juno peeked out from behind Milo's arm. "Its arms are so tiny, though."

Milo burst out laughing. "Huge teeth, tiny arms. That's so funny!"

The giant dinosaur stomped off through the ferns, hunting for its lunch somewhere else.

"Phew," said Juno. "Glad it wasn't hunting us."

"It's just walking by," said the brick gently. "We're only visiting. Nobody here is our lunch."

Juno laughed so hard she fell backward into the soft dirt.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Spiky Tail
chapters.text:
Next, they found a dinosaur with big plates on its back, like stone sails sticking straight up.

"Whoa," said Milo. "What are those plates for?"

"Nobody knows for sure," said the brick. "But look at its tail!"

Juno peeked around the side. Four long spikes stuck out the end. "POINTY!" she shouted.

"Those spikes have a funny name," said the brick. "Scientists call them a **thagomizer**. It just means the spiky part at the end of the tail."

Juno tried the word. "Thuh... gah... mizer!"

Milo laughed so hard he snorted. "Say it again!"

"THAGOMIZER!" Juno yelled, and even the ferns seemed to giggle with her.

The dinosaur swished its spiky tail, slow and proud, and ambled off into the trees.

"Best word ever," said Milo, still grinning.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Wings and Water
chapters.text:
The ferns opened onto a big, shining lake. Something glided overhead, its wings wide and leathery.

"Is that a dinosaur?" Milo asked, shading his eyes.

"Nope," said the brick. "That's a **pterosaur**. It can fly, but it is not a dinosaur. Just a cousin, like your own cousins who look a bit like you."

A tiny creature with four wings swooped between two trees.

"FOUR wings?" Juno said, eyes huge.

"That's Microraptor," said the brick. "Four wings help it glide from tree to tree."

Milo looked at the water. A long, sleek shape swam past, smooth as a shark.

"Is that a shark?" he asked, leaning forward.

"Close," said the brick. "That's a mosasaur. It swims the sea like a shark does, but it's a reptile, not a dinosaur, and not a fish either."

Milo grinned wide. "Sharks are still cooler. Sorry, mosasaur."

"We'll let that one slide," clicked the brick, and Juno giggled at the splash it left behind.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Footprints and Babies
chapters.text:
They walked along a muddy riverbank. Juno stopped short. "Look! A giant footprint!"

Milo knelt beside it. Three big toes pressed deep into the mud.

"The mud got hard, like stone," said the brick. "So the footprint stayed, a long, long time."

"So it never goes away?" Juno asked.

"Exactly," said the brick. "It's like a stamp that never rubs off."

Further along, they found a cozy nest full of round eggs. A gentle dinosaur sat close by, watching.

"That is Maiasaura," said the brick. "Her name even means 'good mother lizard.' She watches her babies, just like your own mom and dad watch you."

Juno waved softly, careful to stay back. "Hi, baby dinosaurs."

"We just look," Milo reminded her. "No touching nests."

"Good dinosaur manners," said the brick, clicking with pride.

Juno sat down quietly and watched the mother dinosaur a while, smiling the whole time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Diggers of Old Bones
chapters.text:
The brick hummed, and the world flickered forward in time.

They landed near a tent in a sandy desert. People knelt in the dirt, brushing dust off big old bones.

"Where are we?" Milo asked.

"This is the **Gobi Desert**," said the brick. "One of the best places on Earth to find old dinosaur bones. A bone that turns hard like rock, after a long, long time underground, is called a **fossil**."

A woman smiled and held up a tiny brush. "I'm a **paleontologist**," she said. "That means I dig up old bones to learn how dinosaurs lived."

"Can I dig too?" Milo asked.

She handed him a soft brush. He swept dirt off a huge tooth, slow and careful.

"Nice find!" she said, clapping once.

The brick clicked proudly. "One of the biggest T. rex skeletons ever found got a nickname. People call her Sue. She turned up in **1990**."

"There's even a story," the brick added, "about a farmer's dog who once dug up a piece of a fossil. That part might just be a fun tale, not something that really happened. But it sure is fun to tell."

Juno giggled. "A doggy paleontologist!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Big Change
chapters.text:
The sky flashed bright, far off, like a giant flashbulb. The brick hummed low and slow.

"A long time after this," said the brick gently, "something huge happened. A giant rock fell from way up in space. It changed the whole world, and most dinosaurs could not live anymore."

Juno's lip wobbled, just a little. "None at all?"

"Not quite none," said the brick. "Some small, feathery dinosaurs lived on. Today, we call them birds. Every robin, every sparrow, is a tiny dinosaur, still flying around."

Juno looked up. Right on cue, a little bird chirped in a branch overhead.

"So dinosaurs never really left," Milo said, grinning. "They just got small and grew wings."

"Exactly," said the brick. "Time to go home now. Ready?"

"WHOOOOSH!" they both shouted.

The world spun back into green carpet and warm lamp light. The LEGO tower still stood tall in the corner.

On the rug sat something new: a tiny LEGO Triceratops, three horns and all, clicked together from leftover bricks.

Juno hugged her plastic dinosaur tight. Milo set the new LEGO one right next to his shark.

"Best trip ever," Milo whispered.

The brick gave one last happy click, then dimmed down to sleep.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: Dinosaurs first showed up about **230 million years ago** — that's a lot of birthdays!
The word **dinosaur** means 'terrible lizard,' because the scientist who named them thought they looked fierce.
**Triceratops** had three horns and a bony collar called a **frill** to protect its neck.
**T. rex** teeth could grow up to **twelve inches long** — almost as long as a ruler and a half!
A **pterosaur** could fly, but it wasn't actually a dinosaur — just a cousin.
**Microraptor** had four wings and could glide between trees.
A **mosasaur** swam in the sea like a shark, but it was a reptile, not a dinosaur.
**Maiasaura** was a caring dinosaur mom who watched over her babies in a nest.
The **Gobi Desert** is one of the best places in the world to dig up old dinosaur bones.
A **paleontologist** is a scientist who digs up old bones to learn how dinosaurs lived.
One of the biggest **T. rex** skeletons ever found is nicknamed **Sue**, discovered in **1990**.
Birds flying around today are actually tiny dinosaurs that lived on!

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Back home, Milo and Juno found a tiny new LEGO Triceratops sitting on the rug beside the LEGO shark, and the brick gave one last happy click before dimming to sleep.

story.title: Sam and Gordo Climb the Walls
story.subtitle: A sticky-toed bedtime adventure

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Gecko
chapters.text:
Sam lay on his tummy on the carpet. He watched a little spider walk up his wall.

"Hello, spider," Sam whispered. He always said hello to bugs.

On his windowsill sat his rubber gecko, Gordo. Gordo had been there for weeks, just sitting.

But tonight, Gordo's back lit up. Glowing green, like a nightlight.

"PSSST," said a tiny voice. "Sam. Look at my toes."

Sam sat up fast. "You... talked!"

Gordo wiggled his little rubber feet, which were suddenly not rubber at all. "Real geckos like me have a trick," he said. "My **toes** are covered in **millions of tiny hairs**. So small, you cannot even see them."

Sam pressed his nose to the glass. "That's how you stick to walls?"

"That's how," said Gordo. "Those tiny hairs grab on tight, so I can run straight up glass. I can even walk upside down on your ceiling."

Sam grinned so big it hurt his cheeks. "Show me! Show me everything that climbs!"

Gordo hopped onto Sam's shoulder. He was warm, and a little bit squishy, and smelled like crayons.

"Hold on tight," said Gordo. "Climb high, stick tight!"

The window glowed green. Sam's bedroom wall rippled like water.

And then — **WHOOSH** — Sam and Gordo were standing on a giant pane of glass, with the whole night sky stretched out below them like a blanket.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Spider on the Glass
chapters.text:
A fuzzy little spider was walking straight up the glass. Right next to Sam's foot.

"Hello, spider!" said Sam. He always said hello to bugs.

The spider waved one leg. Then kept right on climbing.

"Look close," said Gordo. "What do you see on her feet?"

Sam squinted. "They look... fuzzy. Like tiny little hairbrushes!"

"Smart eyes," said Gordo. "Spiders have **thousands of tiny hairs** on their feet, just like me. That is why she can climb smooth glass, same as I do."

Sam pressed his own hand flat on the glass. He pushed hard. Then let go.

SQUEAK. His hand slid right down.

"No fair," said Sam. "My hand doesn't have hairy feet."

"And good thing," laughed Gordo. "Our sticky feet are not glue, either. No mess, no goo. I can lift my toes off, one by one, like peeling up a sticker." He showed Sam, peeling each toe off the glass with a tiny POP POP POP.

Sam giggled. "POP POP POP!"

The spider reached the top of the glass pane and gave a little wave goodbye.

"Where does she go now?" asked Sam.

"Wherever she wants," said Gordo. "That's the best part about climbing."

Sam grabbed Gordo's hand. "Let's go see who else climbs!"

The glass rippled again, green and glowing, and the night pulled them forward.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Buzzy, Hooky Wall
chapters.text:
BZZZZZ. A fat little fly landed on the ceiling above them. Upside down. Not falling at all.

"How does it DO that?" Sam asked, flopping his head back to look.

"Its feet ooze out a teeny bit of sticky goo," said Gordo. "Like tiny glue drops. Just enough to hold on tight, right where it lands."

Sam wrinkled his nose. "Glue feet. Gross and cool."

Below them, a line of ants marched up a bumpy brick wall. Then one ant turned onto a smooth window and kept right on going.

Sam watched hard. "Wait. The bricks are bumpy, but the window is smooth. How does the same ant climb BOTH?"

"Keep watching," said Gordo.

Sam saw it. "Its feet look different! On the bumpy wall it uses tiny claws. On the smooth window it uses sticky pads instead!"

"Ant, you clever little thing," said Gordo. "Two tools, one ant. Claws for bumpy. Sticky pads for smooth. It picks whichever works."

Sam clapped his hands. "It's like having sneakers AND slippers!"

Gordo laughed so hard his tail wobbled. "That is exactly it, Sam."

A cockroach scurried by too, doing the very same trick, claws then pads, pads then claws.

"Everybody's got a trick tonight," said Sam happily.

"Everybody does," said Gordo. "Come on. There's a mountain waiting."

The ceiling melted into starlight, and the window became a cliff.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Up the Rocky Cliff
chapters.text:
WHOOSH. Sam's feet landed on a rocky mountain ledge. Wind tugged at his pajamas.

Far above, a shaggy white goat stood on a cliff so steep it looked like a wall.

"That goat is standing on NOTHING," Sam whispered.

"Look at its feet," said Gordo. "Mountain goats have special **hooves**. Hard and tough on the outside edge. Soft and squishy in the middle, so it squishes flat against the rock."

Sam copied the goat, stomping his own foot. "My foot doesn't squish like that."

"Lucky for your shoes," said Gordo.

A flash of fur zipped past them, straight up a tree trunk. A squirrel, climbing like it was nothing at all.

"How come the squirrel doesn't slide down?" asked Sam.

Gordo pointed. "Count its toes, Sam. What's on the end?"

Sam counted. "Claws! Little curvy claws!"

"Right again," said Gordo. "Those claws dig into teeny-tiny bumps and cracks. Bumps so small, your eyes can't even see them. But the squirrel's claws find every single one."

Sam reached out and touched the rough tree bark. "I can't see any bumps."

"Neither can I," said Gordo. "But the squirrel can feel them."

The squirrel reached the top and chattered happily, like it was bragging.

Sam chattered right back at it, and the squirrel seemed delighted.

"Onward," said Gordo, "before it starts raining."

And right on cue, the first fat raindrop went SPLAT on Sam's nose.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Rainy, Slimy Wall
chapters.text:
Rain pattered down, SPLISH SPLASH, on a big green leaf.

A little tree frog sat right in the middle of it. Upside down. Not sliding one bit.

"The leaf is all wet and slippery," said Sam. "How is the frog not falling off?"

"Look at its toes," said Gordo.

Sam leaned close. "They're flat! And kind of gooey!"

"Exactly," said Gordo. "Tree frog toes are flat and a little bit gooey, with a special grippy pattern. Even on wet, slippery leaves, those toes hold tight."

Sam reached down to the puddle below the leaf, where a small snail was gliding up the side of a flowerpot. Smooth, slow, and never falling.

"The snail doesn't even have feet," Sam said. "How does IT stick?"

"It makes its own slime," said Gordo, "and slides along on a slippery trail, squeezing its squishy foot in little ripples. The slime helps it hang on, even upside down."

Sam watched the shiny trail behind the snail. "It's leaving a sparkly road!"

"It sure is," said Gordo.

Sam gently scooted the snail onto a drier leaf, out of a puddle. "There you go, buddy."

"That was kind," said Gordo, smiling. "Bugs like it when you're gentle."

Sam beamed. "I always am."

The rain softened to a drizzle, and far off, something squeaked upside down in the dark.

"Ooh," said Gordo. "That's our next stop."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Upside Down and Straight Up
chapters.text:
Inside a shadowy cave, something small and furry hung from the ceiling.

A bat. Hanging completely upside down, fast asleep.

"Is it stuck?" Sam asked, a little worried.

"Not stuck," said Gordo gently. "Just resting. Bats hang on with curvy little claws on their feet. It's comfy for them, like your favorite blanket is comfy for you."

Sam relaxed. "Oh good. I thought it needed help."

"Bats don't climb fast like me," said Gordo. "But those claw-feet are perfect for hanging all day long."

Outside the cave, something went KNOCK KNOCK KNOCK against a tree trunk.

A woodpecker, climbing straight up the bark, pecking as it went.

"How does it climb without sliding down backwards?" asked Sam.

"Look at its tail," said Gordo.

Sam looked. "It's all stiff! It's leaning on its tail, like a kickstand!"

"You got it," said Gordo. "Its stiff tail props it up, like a third leg. And its toes point two forward, two backward, so it grips the bark from both sides at once."

"Two forward, two back," Sam repeated, wiggling his own fingers to copy it. "Like a high five going the wrong way!"

Gordo laughed. "Exactly like that."

The woodpecker gave one last happy KNOCK, then flew off into the dark.

"That's a lot of climbers tonight," said Sam, yawning just a tiny bit.

"One more stop," said Gordo. "And this one's about you."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Sticky Glove
chapters.text:
The cave melted away, and Sam and Gordo stood on the same big glass pane from the very start.

But now, a grown-up human was climbing right up it. Wearing two round, flat paddles, one on each hand.

"That's a PERSON!" Sam gasped. "On the wall! Like you!"

"Scientists built those paddles," said Gordo. "Back in **2014**, they copied my sticky toes to make sticky pads big enough for human hands. The person presses, and SCHHHK, it grips the glass."

Sam pressed his own hand flat, wishing hard for paddles of his own.

"People even copied my feet to make brand new kinds of sticky tape," Gordo said proudly. "Tape that peels off clean, just like my toes do. Some of it even works for robot feet, way up in space!"

"In SPACE?" Sam's eyes went huge.

"In space," said Gordo. "Glue doesn't work up there. But sticky toe tricks still do."

Sam grinned. "Your feet are kind of the best feet in the whole world."

"Don't tell the squirrel that," Gordo whispered, and they both giggled.

The glass began to glow soft and green, gentler this time, like a nightlight winding down.

"Time for bed," said Gordo. "Climbers need their sleep too."

WHOOSH. Sam's feet touched his own carpet again. His window was just a window. Gordo sat back on the windowsill, rubber once more — except for one tiny wink.

Sam pulled his blanket up and smiled at every bug he knew was out there, climbing walls all night long.

"Climb high," Sam whispered. "Stick tight."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Sam. Climb high, stick tight.

true_facts.text: Geckos like Gordo have **millions of tiny hairs** on their toes, which is how they climb glass and walk on ceilings.
A gecko's sticky feet are not glue. It can peel its toes off **one by one**, with no mess left behind.
Spiders have **thousands of tiny hairs** on their feet too, which is why many spiders can climb smooth glass.
Flies ooze a tiny bit of sticky goo from their feet, like little glue drops, so they can land upside down on ceilings.
Ants and cockroaches use **claws on bumpy walls** and **sticky pads on smooth walls**, switching their tool depending on the surface.
Mountain goats have hooves with a hard edge and a soft, squishy middle that molds to the rock, so they can stand on steep cliffs.
Squirrels climb using **curvy little claws** that dig into tiny bumps and cracks too small for us to see.
Tree frogs have flat, gooey toe pads with a special grippy pattern, which is how they stick to wet, slippery leaves.
Snails glide up walls on a trail of their own slime, squeezing their squishy foot along in little ripples.
Bats hang upside down from cave ceilings using curvy claws on their feet, like a comfy way to rest.
Woodpeckers climb tree trunks by leaning on their stiff tail like a kickstand, with two toes pointing forward and two pointing back.
In **2014**, scientists built sticky paddles, copied from gecko toes, that let a real person climb straight up a glass wall.
Engineers have copied gecko feet to make sticky tape that peels off clean, and even gripping robot feet that work out in space.
