story.title: Finn and Nell and the Jar That Buzzed
story.subtitle: A sticky, buzzy trip to find out where honey comes from.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Jar That Buzzed
chapters.text:
Finn licked the last sticky spot off his toast. Honey. His favorite.

A drop fell on the counter. PLOP.

The drop began to glow. Gold and warm.

Nell looked up from her yellow flower on the windowsill. "Finn. Look."

The honey jar on the shelf started to hum. BZZZZZZ.

Its lid wiggled. Then it popped off. POP!

Out zoomed a tiny bee, striped gold and brown.

"Hello!" she said. "I'm Clover. Want to see where honey comes from?"

Finn blinked. "Bees can talk?"

"Only to kids who love honey toast," said Clover. She winked.

She sprinkled gold dust over them. It tickled like feathers.

WHOOSH! Finn and Nell shrank down, down, down.

Now they were bee-sized, standing on the counter like two tiny giants.

"WE'RE SO SMALL!" shouted Nell.

"Small enough to fly," said Clover. "Hop on my back."

Finn and Nell climbed onto Clover's soft fuzzy back.

She buzzed her wings. BZZZZZZ. Out the window they flew, into the night garden.

Below them, a yellow flower glowed, Nell's favorite color.

"That flower," said Clover, "is where bees start making honey."

She landed them gently on a petal.

A bee was already there, dipping deep into the flower.

"That's a forager," said Clover. "A flower finder. She sucks up sweet flower juice, called **nectar**, with a long tiny straw tongue."

The forager lifted her head. Her tummy looked round and full.

"She doesn't put it in her eating tummy," said Clover. "She has a second tummy, just for nectar. A **honey tummy**!"

Finn patted his own tummy. "I only have one."

"Lucky you," said Clover, "or you'd buzz everywhere you went."

Nell giggled so hard she nearly rolled off the petal.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Mouth-to-Mouth Magic
chapters.text:
Clover buzzed up and over the garden wall. Finn held on tight.

"Hive, straight ahead!" she called.

A little wooden box sat under a tree. Bees zoomed in and out like a busy door.

Inside, it buzzed so loud Nell covered her ears, then laughed.

The forager bee landed next to another bee. She touched her mouth to the other bee's mouth.

"Ew! Are they kissing?" said Finn.

"Sort of," said Clover. "She's giving her the nectar. Mouth to mouth. Like passing a cup of juice."

The new bee took a sip. Her own tummy filled up gold.

"Her spit does something special," said Clover. "It makes the juice sweeter and thicker. A little less watery every time."

Nell watched the nectar move from bee to bee to bee.

"It's a game of tag!" she said. "Sticky tag!"

"That's exactly it," said Clover, smiling.

Finn started counting. "One bee, two bees, three bees touched it!"

"Keep counting," said Clover. "By the time honey is done, lots of bees have helped."

Finn counted all the way to six before he lost track and giggled.

"Teamwork makes it yummy," said Nell, very proud of her new rule.

Clover nodded. "Best rule I've heard all day."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Six-Sided Rooms
chapters.text:
Deep inside the hive, Clover showed them a golden wall.

It was covered in tiny rooms. Hundreds and hundreds of them.

"Whoa," said Finn. "What are those?"

"Honeycomb," said Clover. "Little rooms made of wax, for holding honey."

Nell leaned close and counted with her finger. "One, two, three, four, five, six sides! Every single one!"

"Good counting," said Clover. "Six flat walls, every time. No squished rooms, no wasted space. They fit together perfect, like puzzle pieces."

"It kind of looks like the middle of my yellow flower," said Nell, tracing a shape in the air.

"Bees would agree with you," said Clover. "They love that shape best."

"Where does the wax come from?" asked Finn. "Do they buy it at a store?"

Clover laughed so hard she wobbled. "No stores here. Bees make it themselves, from little flakes on their own tummies."

"Their tummies make WALLS?" said Finn, patting his own tummy again.

"Yours makes rumbles. Theirs make rooms," said Clover.

A house bee scooted past, spreading nectar into an empty room with her head.

"She's filling it up," said Clover. "One room at a time, all day long."

Nell pressed her nose close, very gently, not touching. "It smells like flowers and sunshine."

"That's the best smell in the whole hive," said Clover.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Buzz, Buzz, Dry!
chapters.text:
A whole row of bees lined up next to the wet, shiny nectar.

They all turned around. Then they flapped their wings. Hard.

BZZZZZZZZZZZ!

The sound filled the whole hive, like a tiny engine.

"Why are they doing that?" asked Nell, flapping her own arms to copy them.

"They're fanning it dry," said Clover. "Nectar has lots of water in it. The wind from their wings blows the watery part away."

"Like drying your hair with a hair dryer!" said Finn.

"Just like that," said Clover. "Only it takes lots of bees, fanning together."

Finn flapped his arms as fast as he could. He lasted about five seconds before they got tired.

"How fast do bee wings go?" he huffed.

"About two hundred flaps, every single second," said Clover.

Finn's mouth fell open. "That's SO fast!"

"That's what makes the buzzing sound," said Clover. "All those wings, flapping together."

Nell tried flapping too, giggling the whole time.

"You'd have very tired arms if you tried to keep up," said Clover.

Slowly, the watery nectar turned thicker. Stickier. Goldener.

"It's turning into honey!" said Nell, pointing with a sticky finger she didn't remember dipping anywhere.

"Almost," said Clover. "Just one more step to go."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Wax Lid and the Winter Jar
chapters.text:
The honey in the little room looked thick and gold now. Just right.

A bee walked over and pressed a thin flake of wax over the top. Like a tiny lid.

"She's putting on a cap," said Nell. "Like a jar!"

"Exactly like a jar," said Clover. "That wax lid keeps the honey clean and safe inside."

"Safe from what?" asked Finn.

"From dust. From bugs. From getting runny again," said Clover.

She flew them along the wall. Room after room had the same little wax lid.

"Why do they make SO much?" asked Finn. "That's a lot of honey."

"For winter," said Clover. "When it's cold, flowers stop growing. No flowers means no nectar. So the bees eat the honey they saved."

Nell thought about snow covering her yellow flowers. "That sounds sad for the flowers."

"The flowers come back in spring," said Clover gently. "And the bees are just fine, snug with their honey."

Finn gasped. "Our jar at home never goes bad! Not ever!"

"You're right," said Clover. "Sealed up honey can last a very, very long time. Maybe forever, if nobody opens the lid."

"I open it every morning," said Finn, a little guiltily.

"That's what it's for," laughed Clover.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Queen and Her Giant Family
chapters.text:
Clover led them toward the middle of the hive. Bees crowded in close.

"Everybody wants to see her," said Clover.

In the middle sat one long bee, bigger than the rest.

"Who's that?" whispered Nell.

"The queen," said Clover. "Every hive has exactly one."

"What does she do? Is she bossy?" asked Finn.

"Not bossy. Busy," said Clover. "Her whole job is laying eggs. Sometimes over a thousand in one single day."

Nell's eyes went huge. "A THOUSAND? That's more than I can count!"

"Way more," laughed Clover. "And almost all those eggs grow up into girl bees. Worker bees. They do every single job here — finding flowers, making wax, fanning honey, guarding the door."

"All the bees we met today were girls?" asked Nell.

"Every one," said Clover proudly.

Finn looked around at the crowd. "How many bees even live here?"

"In summer, a hive can hold tens of thousands," said Clover. "Maybe twenty thousand. Maybe sixty thousand."

Finn tried to count the bees buzzing past. He got to eleven and gave up, laughing.

"That's a LOT of sisters," said Nell.

"One enormous, buzzing family," said Clover.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Waggle Dance Clue
chapters.text:
Near the door, one bee wiggled in a funny little loop. Side to side, round and round.

Finn burst out laughing. "Is she dancing?"

"She is," said Clover. "That's a scout bee. A look-out who already found good flowers. Her wiggly dance tells other bees which way to fly, and how far."

"Can we do it?" asked Nell.

"Try it," said Clover.

Finn wiggled one way. Nell wiggled the other way. They bumped into each other and tumbled over, laughing.

"Follow MY dance," said the scout bee, and zoomed out the door.

Clover, Finn, and Nell followed her, out into the garden.

She led them to a patch of flowers, bright and yellow, Nell's favorite color in the whole world.

"You found it!" cheered Nell, spinning in a circle of her own.

As bees landed on the flowers, golden dust stuck to their fuzzy legs.

"What's that dust?" asked Finn.

"Pollen," said Clover. "When bees carry it from flower to flower, it helps new flowers grow, and fruit too."

"So bees help the whole garden," said Nell softly.

"They sure do," said Clover. "And here's a funny thing. It takes about twelve bees, working their whole lives, just to make one teaspoon of honey."

Finn thought of his toast. "That's a LOT of work for one bite."

"Worth every bit," said Clover.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again, Sticky and Sleepy
chapters.text:
The sky was turning soft and dark. Clover flew them back toward the window.

"One more stop," she said, landing by a little wooden box in the garden.

A person in a big hat and gloves lifted its lid, slow and gentle.

"That's a beekeeper," said Clover. "She takes care of hives like this one. She takes a little honey for people, but always leaves plenty for the bees."

"That seems fair," said Nell.

"Bees think so too," said Clover.

Then she sprinkled gold dust over Finn and Nell again. It tickled like feathers.

WHOOSH! They grew and grew, back to their very own sizes.

They were standing on the kitchen counter again, in their pajamas, right where they started.

The honey jar sat on the shelf, lid back on tight.

"Thank you, Clover," said Finn, through a yawn.

"Anytime," buzzed Clover from somewhere near the window. "Sweet dreams, you two. Buzz well."

Nell climbed into Finn's arms for a hug, smelling faintly of flowers and honey.

On the counter, one last golden drop caught the moonlight.

It looked a little like it was winking goodnight.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Finn. Goodnight, Nell. Buzz well.

true_facts.text: A **forager** bee flies to flowers and sips sweet juice called **nectar** with a long tongue, like a tiny straw.
The nectar goes into a special **honey tummy**, a different tummy than the one she eats with.
Back at the hive, bees pass the nectar **mouth to mouth**, like sharing a cup of juice.
Each time it gets passed along, bee spit makes the nectar sweeter and a little less watery.
Honey is stored in tiny wax rooms with exactly **six flat sides**, called honeycomb.
Bees flap their wings hard to blow the watery part away, turning runny nectar into thick, sticky honey.
Once honey is ready, bees press a thin **wax lid** over the top to keep it clean and safe.
Bees save up honey so they have food to eat in winter, when there are no flowers to visit.
Sealed-up honey can last an extremely long time without ever going bad.
Every hive has one **queen bee**, and she can lay over a thousand eggs in a single day.
A hive can hold tens of thousands of bees in the summer, and almost all of them are girls.
A **scout bee** does a wiggly dance to tell other bees which way to fly to find good flowers.
It takes about twelve bees, working their whole lives, to make just one teaspoon of honey.
A **beekeeper** gently takes a little honey from a hive, but always leaves plenty behind for the bees.

story.title: Omar and the Bicycle That Remembered Everything
story.subtitle: A glowing bell, a wobbly giant wheel, and two hundred years of two-wheeled history.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Ring Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Omar was supposed to be asleep. Instead he sat on his floor, watching clips of his best BMX tricks.

His bike leaned against the wall. Its bell glinted in the dark.

Then the bell started to glow. Green light pulsed, bright as a firefly.

"Psst," said the bell. "Wanna see where bikes began?"

Omar blinked. "Did my bell just talk?"

"Call me Ring," said the bell. "Hop on. First stop: Germany, **1817**."

The bike hummed. WHOOOOSH! The walls melted into dirt roads.

A man wobbled past on a wooden two-wheeler. It had handlebars — but no pedals at all.

"That's **Karl von Drais**," said Ring. "He built the very first bike. People called it a 'running machine,' because you push it along with your feet, like a scooter."

Omar laughed. "That's basically scooting on two wheels!"

He hopped down, balanced like he does at the skate park, and pushed off with one foot. He glided in a perfect straight line.

"Whoa," said Karl, impressed. "You're a natural."

"Years of practice," said Omar. "Just usually with pedals."

Ring's bell chimed happily. "One stop down. Many more to go!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Rattly Ride
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH! The scene changed. Cobblestones rattled under Omar's teeth.

A man rolled past, running the bike with his feet, just like Karl did.

"Still no pedals?" Omar said. "What if you put little pedals right on the front wheel? Like pegs on my BMX!"

Ring's bell flashed. "Funny you say that. **Pierre Michaux** and **Pierre Lallement** did exactly that, in the **1860s**. They called it the velocipede."

"But everyone called it the 'boneshaker,'" Ring laughed, "because cobblestones shook your bones loose!"

Omar grinned, rubbing his teeth. "I believe it."

"Lallement even got a US patent for it, in **1866**," said Ring.

"My idea, basically," said Omar.

"Basically," Ring agreed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Giant Wheel
chapters.text:
A shadow stretched across the road. Omar looked up — way up.

A bicycle rolled by with a front wheel taller than a grown-up, and a tiny wheel behind.

"That's a **penny-farthing**," said Ring. "Named after two old coins — one big, one tiny."

"One turn of the pedal and you fly," said the rider, tipping his hat. "Want a try?"

Omar used his skate-park balance trick, hopping up smooth as anything.

"Careful," Ring warned. "Riders sometimes tipped forward and landed on their heads. They called it 'taking a header.'"

"No headers for me," said Omar, wobbling, then steadying. "Balance is my whole thing."

The rider clapped. "Natural talent!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Chains and Air Pillows
chapters.text:
CLUNK. Omar's wheels jolted over every bump.

"Ouch," he said. "This still hurts."

A man rolled up on a bike with two same-size wheels and a chain, just like Omar's BMX. "**John Kemp Starley**," he said. "I call it the Safety Bicycle. **1885**. Much easier to ride than that wobbly giant wheel."

"Finally, a chain!" said Omar. "But my teeth are still rattling."

"Hmm," said a man nearby, tinkering with a tricycle tire. "I'm **John Boyd Dunlop**. Trying to smooth my son's ride."

Omar thought of his basketball. "What if the tire had air inside, like a ball?"

Dunlop's eyes went wide. "Air inside the rubber! Genius!" In **1888**, he built it for real.

Omar's next bump felt like floating.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Bicycle Craze
chapters.text:
Streets overflowed with bikes. Bells dinged everywhere.

"The **1890s** were the Golden Age," said Ring. "Millions of bikes, sold everywhere."

A woman zoomed past wearing baggy trousers instead of a long skirt.

"Those are bloomers," Ring explained. "Long skirts could get caught in the chain, so riders switched to something safer."

"Bikes gave me somewhere to go, all by myself," the woman called back. "A famous lady named **Susan B. Anthony** said bicycles did more to set women free than almost anything else."

Omar watched her pedal off, fast and free. "That's actually kind of huge," he said.

"Bikes change more than legs," said Ring. "They change lives."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Bike Shop in Dayton
chapters.text:
Metal tools clinked in a small, oily workshop.

"Welcome," said a man fixing a wheel. "I'm **Wilbur Wright**. That's my brother, **Orville**."

Omar spotted thin metal tubes and spoked wheels, light as anything. "Could this stuff work for something besides bikes?"

Orville grinned. "Funny question. We used these same tricks — light metal tubing, spoked wheels — to help build something new."

"In **1903**," Wilbur added, "we flew the first real airplane."

Omar's jaw dropped. "Bike guys built the first plane?!"

"Bike guys," Orville said proudly, "build all sorts of things."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Dirt Track
chapters.text:
Dust kicked up. Bikes soared off dirt jumps nearby.

"Now THIS," said Omar, "is my kind of history."

"**BMX bikes** showed up in the **1970s**," said Ring, "copying motorcycle dirt racing."

Omar spotted riders bombing down a rocky hill on fat, bumpy tires. "Those tires look tough."

"**Mountain bikes**," said Ring, "built the same decade, in California, for rough trails."

"Gears got smarter too," Ring added. "By the **1930s**, riders could shift gears to beat hills. And since **1903**, racers have pedaled the Tour de France — about **3,500 kilometers** across France!"

"That's basically forever," Omar said.

"Today there are over a **billion bikes** on Earth," said Ring. "Some racing bikes weigh less than **8 kilograms** — lighter than your backpack!"

Omar did a quick wheelie, right there in the dust. "Two hundred years," he said, "and it's still awesome."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Bedroom
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH! The dust and dirt faded.

Omar blinked. He was back on his bedroom floor, his bike leaning right where he'd left it.

The bell gave one last soft glow. "Good ride?" asked Ring.

"Best one ever," Omar said, yawning. "Running machines, boneshakers, giant wheels, airplanes..."

"Not bad," said Ring, "for one bell and two wheels."

Omar climbed into bed, already dreaming of tomorrow's tricks — and two hundred years of riders who came before him.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Omar. Ride well.

true_facts.text: The very first bike, built in **1817**, had no pedals — you pushed it along with your feet.
In the **1860s**, inventors added pedals to the front wheel, making the bumpy 'boneshaker.'
A pedal bicycle was patented in the US in **1866**.
The **penny-farthing** had a giant front wheel and a tiny back wheel, named after two old coins.
Penny-farthing riders could tip forward and fall, a tumble nicknamed 'taking a header.'
In **1885**, the Safety Bicycle had two same-size wheels and a chain, like bikes today.
In **1888**, air-filled rubber tires made rides much smoother.
The **1890s** were a bicycle craze, with millions of bikes sold.
Bikes helped give women new freedom to go places on their own.
Long skirts were swapped for safer bloomers so they wouldn't catch in the bike chain.
The Wright brothers ran a bicycle shop before building the first airplane in **1903**.
They used bike-building tricks, like light metal tubing, to help design their flying machine.
**BMX bikes** became popular in the **1970s**, inspired by motorcycle dirt racing.
There are more than a **billion bikes** on Earth today.

story.title: Ada and the Magnet Robot
story.subtitle: A fridge-magnet, a tiny robot, and the invisible pull that holds the whole world together

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Wobbly Magnet
chapters.text:
Ada sat on her bedroom rug, snapping fridge magnets into a tiny robot body. She had done this every night this week.

She pushed two magnets together. CLUNK! They snapped tight, like best friends.

She flipped one around and pushed again. The magnets would not touch. They slid apart, like they were cross with each other.

"Why won't you stick?" Ada said.

A hum rose from her pile. One magnet lifted off the rug, spun, and grew two blinking eyes.

"Because," said the tiny robot, "every magnet has two ends, called poles — one north, one south. North and south like each other. North and north push apart. So do south and south."

Ada flipped her magnet back. CLICK! It snapped tight again.

"IT STICKS!" she shouted, rolling onto her back, laughing.

"I'm Clink," said the robot, spinning happily. "Want to see more magnet magic? Hop on."

Ada climbed aboard. The ceiling swirled into stars, and her bedroom melted away.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Invisible Hug
chapters.text:
Clink zoomed into a kitchen stuffed with sparkly dust. "Watch this," he said, and shook a jar over the table.

Tiny black bits — iron filings, which are just tiny bits of metal — landed near a magnet.

They didn't just sit there. They swooped into curvy lines, from one end to the other.

"Whoa!" Ada said. "They're drawing a picture!"

"That's the magnet's invisible hug," said Clink. "We call it a **magnetic field**. It's the space around the magnet where its pull and push work, even though you can't see it."

Ada dragged a spoon through the dust, then held the magnet near it. The bits swirled into a heart shape, right between the two ends.

"IT MADE A HEART!" Ada yelled, clapping.

"Lucky guess," said Clink, "or magnet magic. Probably both."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Tiny Spinning Dancers
chapters.text:
Next stop: a pile of odds and ends — a wooden spoon, a penny, a gold ring, a steel paperclip.

"Why do some things stick and some don't?" Ada asked, holding her magnet near each one.

"Inside everything are tiny, tiny bits called atoms," Clink said. "Inside those are even tinier bits called electrons, spinning around like little tops."

"In magnets, all those spinning bits line up the same way, like dancers doing the same move. That teamwork makes a strong pull."

Ada touched the magnet to the paperclip. CLICK! It jumped right up.

She tried the gold ring. Nothing happened.

"Gold's little dancers point every which way," said Clink. "No teamwork, no stick."

"So gold is the lazy dancer," Ada giggled, "and iron does gym class."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Rock That Pointed
chapters.text:
Fog cleared into a hillside, where a dusty gray rock sat glowing faintly.

"This is a lodestone," said Clink, "a special rock that's magnetic all by itself."

"Long, long ago, people in Greece found rocks like this near a place called Magnesia," he said. "That might be where the word magnet came from, though nobody's fully sure."

Ada tied a string around the rock and let it dangle. It swung, then stopped — always pointing the same way.

"It's like an arrow!" Ada said.

"Smart catch," said Clink. "More than two thousand years ago, people in China used rocks just like this to make the very first **compasses** — tools that always point the same way, to help travelers find their path."

Ada spun the rock. It settled back to the same spot every single time.

"IT ALWAYS KNOWS THE WAY!" she shouted.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Giant Magnet Called Earth
chapters.text:
They floated up, up, until the whole blue planet hung below them like a marble.

"Why does a compass always point the same way, everywhere?" Ada asked.

"Because the whole Earth is a giant magnet," said Clink. "Deep, deep down, melted metal swirls around, and that swirling makes a magnetic field that wraps the entire planet."

Ada pulled a tiny toy compass from her pocket. "If I spin it, it has to point north, right?"

She spun it. It wobbled, then settled. North.

"TOLD YOU!" Ada cheered.

Clink spun too, dizzy and delighted. "A scientist named Oersted once saw a compass needle wiggle near a wire buzzing with electricity. Nobody expected that. Turned out electricity and magnets are secret friends."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Switch It On!
chapters.text:
They landed in a clanky junkyard, where a giant arm swung overhead on a crane.

"Watch what happens when I flip this switch," said Clink.

Ada flipped it. The crane's round head buzzed, and a heap of old cars lifted clean off the ground.

"That's an **electromagnet**," said Clink. "You wrap wire into a loop, run electricity through it, and it turns into a magnet — one you can switch on and off."

"OFF, please!" Ada giggled, and flipped it back. The cars lowered down gently, with a soft CLUNK.

"Doorbells use these too," said Clink. "So do loudspeakers, and the motors that spin all sorts of machines."

Ada grinned. "So a crane and my doorbell are basically magnet cousins."

"Basically," said Clink. "Stick with me, there's more."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Home Again
chapters.text:
The junkyard melted away, and the rug came back under Ada's knees.

Clink floated down, smaller now, blinking slow sleepy blinks.

"One more trick," he said. He took a toy bar magnet and snapped it in half. CRACK!

Ada gasped. "Did you break the magnet magic?"

"Nope," said Clink. "Cut a magnet in half, and each piece becomes its very own little magnet, with a north end and a south end, both all over again."

Ada pressed her fridge-magnet robot onto the fridge door. It bent a little, then held tight.

"Fridge magnets are squishy rubber mixed with magnet powder," said Clink. "That's why they bend without ever losing their stick."

Ada yawned a huge yawn. Clink settled onto her pillow, glowing soft and low.

"Stick with me tomorrow?" he whispered.

"Always," Ada mumbled, already half asleep.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ada. Stick with me, always.

true_facts.text: A magnet has two ends, a **north** end and a **south** end, where the pull is strongest.
Two norths push apart, two souths push apart, but a **north and a south stick together**.
The space around a magnet where its push and pull work is called a **magnetic field**.
Tiny bits of metal called **iron filings** swoop into curvy lines when they land near a magnet.
Inside everything are tinier bits called **electrons**, and in magnets they all spin the same way, like dancers doing the same move.
Shiny **gold** does not stick to an ordinary magnet, because its tiny spinning bits don't team up.
A special rock called a **lodestone**, found by ancient Greeks near a place called Magnesia, is magnetic all by itself.
More than **two thousand years ago**, people in China used lodestones to make the first **compasses**.
Deep inside, the whole **Earth** is swirling with melted metal, which makes it act like a giant magnet.
A compass needle always settles pointing **north**, because it lines up with Earth's magnetic pull.
An **electromagnet** is made by wrapping wire into a loop and running electricity through it, and it can be switched on and off.
Electromagnets are used in **doorbells**, loudspeakers, motors, and giant **cranes** that lift old cars.
If you **cut a magnet in half**, each new piece becomes its own little magnet, with a north and south end again.
**Fridge magnets** are made from bendy rubber mixed with magnet powder, so they can bend without losing their stick.

story.title: Priya, Dev, and the Rainbow Water Pistol
story.subtitle: A squirt, a sunbeam, and seven secret colors.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Squirt That Made a Rainbow
chapters.text:
Priya was painting a sun on paper. Dev was filling his water pistol in the bathroom sink, which he was absolutely, definitely allowed to do.

"Watch this," Dev said, and squirted a spray right across the sunbeam coming through the window.

A tiny bow of colors popped into the air — red, then orange, then a smear of blue. It hung there, over the carpet, for one whole second.

"WHOA," said Priya, dropping her paintbrush. "Do it again!"

Dev squirted again. Nothing. He squirted toward the dark corner. Nothing.

"You need the sun **behind** you," said a small, fizzy voice, "and the water spray in **front**." A bead of light popped out of the mist like a soap bubble that forgot how to pop. "Sun and water, both at once — that's the whole trick. I'm Fizz."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Bendy Light Trick
chapters.text:
Fizz floated over the sink, blinking like a tiny flashlight.

"Why does my spray turn into colors?" Dev asked, squeezing the trigger again.

"Sunlight goes into each drop of water," said Fizz, "and it bends. That's called **refraction**. Bending light, that's all it means."

Priya raised her paintbrush like a magic wand. "So light turns a corner inside the water?"

"Exactly," said Fizz. "Light moves slower in water than in air. So it tips sideways, just a little."

Dev squirted a long, steady stream. He held his pistol dead still. The colors held for three whole seconds.

"RECORD BREAKER," Priya announced, and gave her brother a high five.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Newton's Secret Stripe
chapters.text:
Fizz led them through the window, which shimmered into swirling light instead of glass.

They landed in a dusty room, full of sunlight.

A man in a long coat held up a triangle of glass. "Watch," he said, tipping it into a sunbeam.

A stripe of colors spilled across the table.

"That's **Isaac Newton**," whispered Fizz. "In **1666**, he used a glass triangle, called a **prism**, to prove sunlight secretly holds every color."

Priya counted on her fingers. "Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet! Like my paint box, but in order!"

"Red sits on the outside," said Newton. "Violet squeezes in on the inside. Red bends the least. Violet bends the most."

Dev squinted at the glowing stripe. "So my rainbow is just Newton's trick. But squirtier."

Newton laughed so hard his wig wobbled.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Donut in the Sky
chapters.text:
Fizz swooped them up high, above fluffy clouds.

"Where did the ground go?" asked Dev, nose pressed to an imaginary window.

"That's the point," said Fizz. "A rainbow is actually a whole circle. The **ground usually blocks the bottom half**, so we only see an arch."

Below them, a perfect ring of color floated in the open sky, like a donut made of light.

"IT'S A CIRCLE!" shouted Priya. "Like a hula hoop!"

"People flying in airplanes sometimes see this," said Fizz. "No ground in the way."

Dev pointed his water pistol at a misty cloud below and squirted. A tiny circle rainbow popped up around the spray.

"Pilot Dev, reporting a perfect donut," he said, saluting.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Your Rainbow, My Rainbow
chapters.text:
Back on solid ground, rain fell in a nearby field.

Priya stood by a fence. Dev stood ten steps to her left.

"I see the rainbow over the big tree," said Priya.

"Mine's over the barn," said Dev. "We're looking at the SAME rainbow, right?"

"Nope," said Fizz. "Every person sees their **own** rainbow, made from different raindrops. It depends on the exact angle between the sun, the water, and your eyes."

"So I have a Priya rainbow and you have a Dev rainbow?" Priya grinned. "Mine's obviously better."

"Is not," said Dev, sticking out his tongue.

Above the first bow, a second, fainter one appeared, its colors flipped upside down.

"A **double rainbow**," said Fizz. "Light bounces twice inside some drops, so the colors reverse."

"Double trouble," said Priya, "double awesome."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Bridge, the Promise, and the Gold
chapters.text:
Fizz carried them to a cold, windy bridge made of shimmering color.

"Welcome to **Bifrost**," said Fizz. "Old Norse stories tell of a rainbow bridge. It connects earth to the home of the gods."

Dev stomped on it. His foot went right through the mist.

"Another old story," Fizz said gently, "says a rainbow is a sign of a promise. It comes after a big flood, in the story of Noah."

"Irish stories tell of a pot of gold at the rainbow's end," Fizz went on, "watched by tiny magical **leprechauns**. That part is probably just a fun tale. But it shows how much people loved rainbows."

Dev sprinted toward the glowing end of the arch. He ran and ran. The end kept moving away.

"You can never actually reach a rainbow," said Fizz, laughing. "It moves whenever you move. Sorry, no gold today."

"Worth a try," panted Dev.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Rainbows Hiding Everywhere
chapters.text:
Fizz zoomed them past a roaring waterfall, sparkling with tiny rainbows in its mist.

"Rainbows hide in all sorts of watery places," said Fizz. "Waterfalls, garden hoses, foggy mist. Even moonlight makes a ghostly pale one, called a **moonbow**."

"Our eyes can't see much color in a moonbow," Fizz added. "But a camera can catch it."

Priya tilted her head. "So science is basically everywhere, hiding in splashes?"

"That's called **optics**," said Fizz. "The part of science about how light moves, bends, and bounces."

Dev squirted his pistol one more time, toward the waterfall's mist. A tiny rainbow joined the big one, right beside it.

"Mine counts too," Dev said proudly.

"Every drop counts," said Fizz.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Sun and Water, Both at Once
chapters.text:
Fizz carried them back through the swirl of light, straight into the bathroom.

Priya's paintbrush lay exactly where she had dropped it. Dev's water pistol dripped in his hand.

"Sun behind you, water in front," Dev said. "That's the whole secret."

"And it's secretly made of every color," Priya said, picking up her brush, "even when it looks plain white."

On her paper, instead of a plain yellow sun, she painted a full, glowing circle. A rainbow with no ground to block it.

Dev squirted one last gentle spray across the sunbeam. A tiny, perfect arc popped up, hovered a moment, and faded.

"Goodnight bow," he whispered.

Fizz winked out like a dying sparkler. "Sun and water, kiddos. See you next time."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Priya. Goodnight, Dev. Sun and water, both at once.

story.title: Jack, Ellie, and the Mermaid's Purse
story.subtitle: One glowing shell, one long night, and five hundred kinds of shark.

chapters.heading: Chapter One: The Glowing Purse
chapters.text:
Jack lay on his bedroom floor, lining up seven shark teeth he'd found at the beach. Ellie sat next to him, turning a small brown pouch over in her hands. It was shaped like a seashell, flat and leathery, with curly strings on each corner.

"It's a mermaid's purse," Ellie said. "Mermaids keep their coins in it."

"It's not a real purse," said Jack. "It's just a shell thing."

"Is too a purse."

"Is not."

Then the little purse started to glow. Green light leaked out between Ellie's fingers like water finding a crack. Jack froze, his hand still on his biggest tooth.

"Jack," Ellie whispered, "it's doing the thing."

The glow spread across the carpet, turning it into swirling, see-through water. A doorway opened in the middle of the room, and through it they could see the deep blue sea.

"Don't let go of it," Jack said, grabbing Ellie's hand. Together they stepped through.

They landed softly on sand at the bottom of the ocean, somehow breathing just fine. A gray shape slid past them, bending its whole body in one smooth curve.

"How does it bend like that?" Jack asked, poking the air where it had been.

The purse glowed warm in Ellie's hand and a voice like popping bubbles answered. "A shark's skeleton isn't hard bone like yours," it said. "It's made of **cartilage** — bendy stuff, like the soft part of your ear. That's why sharks curve so easily."

"Whoa," said Jack, bending his own ear to check.

"There are more than **500 kinds of sharks** swimming around today," the purse added. "Big ones, tiny ones, all sorts."

"Five hundred?" Ellie counted on her fingers and gave up after ten. "That's a LOT of sharks."

"Let's meet some," said Jack, already swimming ahead.

chapters.heading: Chapter Two: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
A shadow bigger than their house slid over the sand. It blocked out the sunlight like a cloud.

Ellie grabbed Jack's arm. "Is it going to eat us?"

Jack looked up. A gray shape as long as a school bus glided past, its mouth open wide.

"No teeth," Jack said. "Just a big hole."

The purse bubbled warm in Ellie's hand. "That's a whale shark," it said. "The biggest fish in the whole sea. It can grow over **40 feet long** — longer than a school bus."

"Then why isn't it eating us?" Ellie asked, peeking from behind Jack's shoulder.

"It only eats plankton," said the purse. "Tiny floating bits of food, smaller than a grain of rice. It just opens its mouth and swallows a whole gulp of seawater, bits and all."

Jack grinned and swam a little closer, careful not to touch. "That's like drinking soup through a straw the size of a door."

The whale shark's eye rolled toward them, calm and unbothered.

"How old do you think it is?" Jack asked, counting the pale spots scattered across its back like stars.

"Some whale sharks live past **100 years old**," said the purse. "Older than almost anyone you know."

Ellie's mouth fell open. "That's older than Grandpa!"

"Way older," said Jack, laughing so hard he blew bubbles.

The whale shark gave one slow flick of its tail and swam on.

"See?" Jack said. "Big doesn't mean scary."

Ellie let go of his arm, just a little. "Okay. But I'm still holding the purse."

chapters.heading: Chapter Three: Teeth as Long as a Hand
chapters.text:
Jack's foot bumped something hard in the sand. He pulled out a tooth as long as his hand, smooth and shaped like a triangle.

"Whoa," he said. "That's bigger than all seven of mine put together."

Ellie poked it. "What kind of shark has teeth like that?"

The purse glowed low and old, like a light from far away. "That tooth belonged to megalodon," it said. "A giant shark that lived millions of years ago. It isn't around anymore. We call that **extinct** — gone for good."

"How do we even know about it, then?" Jack asked, turning the tooth over.

"Mostly from teeth just like that one," said the purse. "A shark's bendy insides rarely last. But hard teeth can turn into **fossils** — old shapes kept safe in rock or sand — for a very, very long time."

"Sharks were swimming around before dinosaurs," the purse added. "More than **400 million years** before trees even grew on land."

Ellie tried to imagine a number that big and gave up. "That's older than EVERYTHING."

Jack counted his own teeth with his tongue. "Wait — do shark teeth keep growing back if one falls out?"

"They do," said the purse. "A shark can lose and grow **thousands of teeth** in its life. New ones are always moving up to take the old one's place, like a conveyor belt."

"Lucky," said Jack. "I only get two tries."

Ellie giggled so hard a bubble popped right out of her nose.

chapters.heading: Chapter Four: Sandpaper Skin and Hammer Heads
chapters.text:
A small shark brushed past Ellie's arm. She yelped and yanked her hand back.

"It felt like sandpaper!" she said, rubbing her fingers together.

"That's its skin," said the purse. "Covered in tiny bumps called **denticles** — little points smaller than glitter. They make the skin feel rough, but they also help the shark slide through the water fast."

"So sharks are covered in baby teeth?" Ellie asked.

"Sort of," said the purse, and Jack laughed so hard he swallowed a bubble.

Just then something strange swam toward them: a shark with a head shaped like a hammer, flat and wide, with an eye bulging from each end.

"Why's its head like that?" Jack asked, swimming closer for a look.

"It's called a **cephalofoil**," said the purse. "A fancy word for a wide, flat head. It spreads the shark's eyes far apart, so it can see almost all the way around itself."

Ellie waved both arms out to the sides, trying to copy it. "Can I see behind me now?"

"Not quite," said Jack, grinning. "You'd need the actual hammer head."

The hammerhead swung its strange head side to side, scanning the sand below, then swam off without a second glance.

"Weird," said Ellie, still rubbing her sandpapery fingers. "But kind of cool weird."

chapters.heading: Chapter Five: The Walking Shark and the Fastest Fin
chapters.text:
Something was walking across the coral. Actually walking, on four stubby fins like legs.

Jack stopped swimming. "Sharks can't walk."

"This one can," said the purse. "It's called an **epaulette shark**. It uses its paddle-shaped fins to flip over the reef, almost like little feet."

Ellie watched it flop-walk over a rock. "Why doesn't it just swim?"

"Sometimes the water gets shallow and trapped at low tide," said the purse. "This shark can last for hours with hardly any air in the water, so it just walks to the next puddle instead."

"That's the laziest, cleverest shark ever," Jack said.

A gray blur shot past them so fast the water shook.

"WHOA! What was THAT?" Jack shouted, spinning around.

"A shortfin mako," said the purse. "The fastest shark in the sea. It uses quick bursts of speed to catch fast fish like tuna."

"Race you to that rock," Jack said to Ellie, already kicking off.

"That's not fair, you dive all the time!" Ellie said, kicking after him anyway.

Neither of them came close to the mako's speed, but they reached the rock laughing, out of breath, the little walking shark still flip-flopping along behind them like it had all the time in the world.

chapters.heading: Chapter Six: The Tingle in the Sand
chapters.text:
Jack buried his hand in the sand, just to see what would happen. A small shark nearby turned sharply and swam straight toward it.

"How'd it know I was there?" Jack asked, yanking his hand back out. "I didn't even move!"

"Sharks have a secret sense," said the purse. "Jelly-filled holes in their snout called the **ampullae of Lorenzini** — tiny sensors that feel electricity. Every living thing makes a little bit, even you, just by moving a muscle."

"So it felt my heartbeat?" Jack asked, pressing a hand to his chest.

"Close enough," said the purse. "It felt your hand twitching in the sand."

Ellie stuck both hands in the sand at once. "Can it feel me too?"

Nothing happened. The purse bubbled with something like a laugh. "Only if you move."

Ellie wiggled her fingers furiously, and sure enough, another small shark drifted over to investigate. It nosed gently at the sand, curious, not hungry, then swam on.

"See?" Jack said. "Not scary. Just nosy."

"Like you," Ellie said, "reading my diary."

"That was ONE time," said Jack, and the purse bubbled with laughter all over again.

chapters.heading: Chapter Seven: The Shark Lady
chapters.text:
Ellie spotted something tucked into a clump of seaweed: another purse, just like hers, but smaller.

"There's more!" she said, scooping it up gently.

"That's a real mermaid's purse," said the purse in her hand. "Some sharks lay eggs inside cases just like that. Other sharks don't lay eggs at all. They have live babies called pups, same as you were a baby once."

"So I was holding a shark egg this whole time?" Ellie asked, delighted.

"You were holding your own magic one," said the purse. "But yes, out in the real ocean, that's just what one looks like."

A new voice bubbled up, warm and curious. "I spent my whole life studying creatures just like these."

"Who's that?" Jack asked.

"**Eugenie Clark**," said the purse. "People called her the Shark Lady. She studied sharks for years and proved they're curious and clever, and can even be trained, not the scary monsters people thought."

"Sharks don't even want to eat people, right?" Jack said, remembering something he'd read.

"Right," said the purse. "Shark attacks on people are extremely rare. Far more sharks get hurt by people than the other way around. Mostly, sharks just keep the ocean healthy, eating the sick and the slow so everything else stays balanced."

Ellie held the tiny purse close. "We should look after them. Like they look after the sea."

"Exactly," said the purse, glowing warm and bright.

chapters.heading: Chapter Eight: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The purse in Ellie's hand began to glow, bright green, same as before.

"I think it's time to go home," Jack said, though he didn't really want to.

"Just one more shark?" Ellie asked.

"Next time," said the purse. "There are still hundreds you haven't met."

The glowing doorway opened again, swirling like water finding a crack, and the ocean dissolved back into bedroom carpet.

Jack and Ellie landed softly, right where they'd started, Jack's seven teeth still lined up in a neat row.

Ellie looked down at the little leathery purse in her hand. It had stopped glowing, but it still felt warm, like it was a tiny bit awake.

"Told you it was a real purse," Ellie said.

Jack opened his mouth to argue, then stopped. "Fine. Maybe it's a little bit a purse."

"A mermaid's purse," said Ellie, "for keeping sharks in."

Jack laughed and set his biggest tooth right next to it on the carpet, tooth and purse together, side by side.

Outside, the night was quiet and the ocean was very far away. But somewhere, a whale shark was still swimming slow circles, older than anybody they knew, and a little walking shark was flip-flopping home across the reef.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Jack. Goodnight, Ellie. Swim well.

There are more than **500 kinds of sharks** swimming in the ocean today.
The whale shark is the biggest fish in the sea, growing over **40 feet long**, but it only eats tiny floating bits called plankton.
Some whale sharks live past **100 years old**, older than almost anyone you know.
**Megalodon** was a giant shark that lived millions of years ago and isn't around anymore.
Sharks were swimming in the ocean more than **400 million years** before dinosaurs or trees ever existed.
A shark can lose and grow back **thousands of teeth** over its life, with new ones always moving up to replace old ones.
Shark skin is covered in tiny bumps called **denticles**, which make it feel like sandpaper and help the shark swim smoothly.
Hammerhead sharks have a wide, flat head called a **cephalofoil** that spreads their eyes apart so they can see all around.
The **epaulette shark** can flip itself across rocks using its fins like little feet, almost like walking.
The **shortfin mako** is the fastest shark in the sea, using quick bursts of speed to catch fast fish.
Sharks can feel tiny bits of electricity from other animals using special sensors in their snout called the **ampullae of Lorenzini**.
Some sharks lay eggs in a leathery case called a **mermaid's purse**, while others have live babies called pups.
Scientist **Eugenie Clark**, nicknamed the Shark Lady, proved that sharks are curious and clever, and can even be trained.

story.title: Nora and the Glowing Tile of Pompeii
story.subtitle: A mosaic piece that remembers a Roman town

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Tile
chapters.text:
Nora sat on her bedroom carpet, gluing tiny colored tiles onto a mosaic coaster. The house was quiet. Everyone else was asleep.

One tile would not glue down right. It felt warm, almost hot, and glowed soft gold.

Nora picked it up. The gold light grew brighter, washing over her room like a wave.

When the light faded, she stood on a stone street. The stones had gaps, with big flat rocks poking up in a row across the road.

"Careful," said a small voice. The tile in her hand was talking now. "Those are stepping stones. People hopped across to keep their feet dry. Carts still rolled through the gaps."

"Where am I?" Nora asked.

"Pompeii," said the tile. "A busy Roman town, near where the city of Naples is today."

Nora hopped onto a stepping stone. Her sneaker fit perfectly. "It works!" she laughed, hopping all the way across like a real Roman kid.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Thirsty Fountain
chapters.text:
Down the street, a stone fountain gurgled. Clear water splashed into a carved basin.

"Where does the water come from?" Nora asked.

"Pipes," said the tile. "Lead pipes, buried under the street, carry water all over town. Fountains like this one give everyone a drink."

A woman filled a clay jug and smiled at Nora.

"How many people live here?" Nora asked.

"About eleven thousand," said the tile. "Shops, bathhouses, temples — this town has everything."

Nora counted the shop doors along the street. She lost count after twenty.

"Busy place!" she said, grinning.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Stone Rings
chapters.text:
A huge oval building rose ahead, like a giant stone bowl.

"What's that?" Nora asked, tipping her head back.

"An amphitheater," said the tile. "A big open stage with seats curving all around. It was built about seventy years before we got here, and people watched games there."

Nora climbed a few worn steps. The seats curved in neat rings, one inside another.

"It's shaped like my coaster!" she said. "Rings inside rings."

"Good eye," said the tile. "You're already thinking like an archaeologist — someone who studies old places to learn how people once lived."

Nora grinned and kept climbing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Baker's Mark
chapters.text:
Down a side street, a baker pulled a round loaf from a stone oven.

He pressed a little stamp into the top. "That's my mark," he said, "so everyone knows whose bread this is."

Nora watched him line up loaf after loaf. "It smells amazing," she said.

"Remember this oven," said the tile quietly. "We'll come back to it."

Nora wondered why. She tucked the mystery away and followed the tile down the street.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Walls That Talked
chapters.text:
Bright paintings covered the walls in reds, golds, and deep blues.

"Frescoes," said the tile. "Paintings made right into wet wall plaster, so the colors never flake off."

Nora traced a swirling pattern with her finger. "It's like a painted mosaic."

In one house, the tile showed her strange, swirling scenes. "That's the Villa of the Mysteries," it said. "Nobody is fully sure what special happening those paintings show. It's still a bit of a mystery."

Further along, bold letters covered a storefront: VOTE FOR MARCUS.

"People painted messages right on their walls," said the tile. "Ads for shops, or names of people they wanted to win elections."

Nora laughed. "Walls were like signs!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Mountain Wakes
chapters.text:
The sky turned strange. Gray clouds piled up over a tall mountain nearby.

"Mount Vesuvius," said the tile, calm but serious. "On August 24th, in the year 79, it woke up."

Nora felt a flutter of worry. "Are we safe?"

"We're only watching," said the tile. "Like Pliny the Younger did, from across the bay. He wrote two long letters about it, so carefully that scientists still use his words today. They even named this kind of eruption after him — a Plinian eruption."

Across the water, his uncle, Pliny the Elder, sailed his ship closer, trying to help people get away. That took real courage.

Soft ash began to fall, gray as snow.

"It happened fast," said the tile. "Too fast to clean up. Ash and rock covered the whole town, piled as deep as a two-story house."

Nora watched quietly, safe inside the gold light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Nearly Seventeen Hundred Years Later
chapters.text:
The gold light shimmered, and the scene changed. Nora stood over a dusty dig.

"In 1748," said the tile, "workers digging nearby found old walls. People had almost forgotten this town was ever here."

Nora watched soft brushes sweep dirt from a painted wall. "They're being so careful."

"That's how archaeologists work," said the tile. "Slow and gentle, so nothing breaks."

"What about that bakery?" Nora asked, remembering.

The tile glowed brighter. "Go look."

Nora peeked into the old oven. Inside sat a loaf of bread, round and stamped, turned hard as stone, baked almost two thousand years ago.

"IT NEVER GOT EATEN!" Nora shouted.

"Not far away," said the tile, "a smaller town called Herculaneum was buried too, under different ash that kept even wooden furniture whole."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Carpet
chapters.text:
"Is Pompeii still there?" Nora asked.

"Yes," said the tile. "Millions of people visit those streets every year now. It's called a World Heritage Site — a place so special the whole world helps protect it."

"Did they find everything?"

"Not yet," said the tile. "New paintings and rooms still turn up."

"And the mountain?"

"Still there," said the tile. "Scientists watch it closely, every single day."

The gold light swirled again. Nora blinked, and she was back on her carpet, her coaster half-finished in her lap.

The little tile sat still now, dark and ordinary — except for one last glimmer, like a wink.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Nora. Dream in mosaic colors.

true_facts.text: Pompeii was a real Roman town, close to where the city of **Naples** is today.
On **August 24th**, in the year **79**, the volcano **Mount Vesuvius** erupted.
About **eleven thousand** people once lived and worked in Pompeii.
The eruption covered the whole town in ash and rock, piled as deep as **a two-story house**.
A young Roman named **Pliny the Younger** watched from far away and wrote it all down — so carefully that this kind of eruption is now called a **Plinian eruption**.
Pompeii was forgotten for a very long time, until workers digging in **1748** found its old walls again.
A nearby town called **Herculaneum** was buried too, and its ash even kept wooden furniture whole.
Some painted walls, called **frescoes**, showed colorful scenes — including mysterious pictures in a house called the **Villa of the Mysteries**.
Pompeii had **pipes** buried under its streets, carrying water to fountains all over town.
The town's big stone **amphitheater**, built about **seventy years** before the eruption, was used for games.
One baker's loaf of bread, still stamped with his mark, was found inside an old oven.
Pompeii's streets had raised **stepping stones**, so people could cross without muddy feet while carts rolled through the gaps.
Mount Vesuvius is still an active volcano, and scientists keep a close watch on it today.
Pompeii is now protected as a **World Heritage Site**, and millions of people visit it every year.

story.title: Maya and the Race to the Stars
story.subtitle: A paper boat, a seal with a pun, and a sky full of firsts.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beeping Ball (1957)
chapters.text:
Maya sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor. Rain tapped the round window above her bed. She was drawing a sailboat, the pencil scratching soft and slow.

It had been one whole week since Barnacle waved a flipper at her from the harbor, the night the big bridge got its very last rivet.

Her bedside bowl still had an inch of rainwater in it from the open window. A paper boat floated there, glowing soft blue, like moonlight caught in paper.

SPLOOSH! A round, whiskered face popped up out of the bowl.

"All aboard, Maya!" said Barnacle the harbor seal, shaking water off his nose.

Maya grinned and folded her drawing into a boat. The moment it touched the water, it grew porthole windows and a curved hull. She climbed aboard, and WHOOOOSH, it rose right out through the window, into the rainy dark, and past the stars.

They bumped down gently on a cloud of crackly static. A little radio nearby kept making a strange, steady sound: beep... beep... beep.

"What's making that noise?" Maya asked, leaning close.

"Count the beeps," said Barnacle.

Maya counted. One, two, three, over and over, never stopping.

"It's not stopping," she said. "Like it's talking."

"That's exactly right," said Barnacle. "It's a satellite — a shiny ball that circles around Earth. This one is called Sputnik 1. On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union sent it up, the very first satellite ever."

Maya peered at a little gold ball drifting past. "It's tiny!"

"About 58 centimeters wide," said Barnacle. "Smaller than your beach ball. But that beep, anyone down on Earth with an ordinary radio could hear it."

Maya pressed her ear to the crackly radio and grinned as the beeps buzzed through her teeth. "I want to see what happens next," she said.

Barnacle's whiskers twitched into a smile. "Then hang onto your hull. There's a lot more sky to see."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Brave Dog in the Sky (1957)
chapters.text:
The little radio crackled, then made a brand-new sound: a soft, high whimper.

Maya sat up straight. "That's not a beep," she said. "That sounds like... a puppy."

Barnacle floated closer, whiskers drooping kindly. "Good ears," he said. "Follow me."

The paper boat tipped sideways, and WHOOOOSH, they sailed past a second, rounder satellite — a shiny ball that circles Earth — with a little window cut into its side.

Inside, a small furry face looked out: perky ears, bright eyes, panting softly.

"A dog! In SPACE?" Maya gasped.

"Her name is Laika," said Barnacle. "On **November 3, 1957**, just a month after Sputnik 1, the Soviet Union sent her up on **Sputnik 2**. She became the very first living creature to go all the way around Earth."

Maya counted the little round windows along the satellite's side: one, two, three. "Is she scared up there all alone?" she asked.

"She's brave," said Barnacle. "Famous too. People everywhere still say her name."

Maya dug in her pocket and found the leftover scrap of her drawing: one small gold star. She smoothed it flat on her knee.

"Can I give her this?" she asked. "So she has company?"

Barnacle's whole face grinned. "Space is big enough for one more gift," he said.

Maya folded the star into a tiny paper boat of its own and let it drift from her fingers. It sailed across the dark, bumped gently against Laika's window, and stuck there like a sticker.

Through the glass, Laika's tail gave one small, happy thump.

"She likes it!" Maya cheered, bouncing on the hull of her own boat.

"Of course she does," said Barnacle. "Everybody likes a surprise star."

The little satellite spun on, carrying its brave passenger and her new gold star, off into the dark on the very first lap any living creature had ever flown around the whole wide world.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Invisible Belt (1958)
chapters.text:
A thin silver needle on a little dial began to twitch. Tick, tick, TICK-tick.

Maya leaned over it. "Barnacle, why is it jumping around like that?"

"Ah," said Barnacle, popping up beside a small, pencil-shaped satellite. "That needle is counting something you cannot see."

"Something I can't see is hard to count," said Maya, frowning.

"That's exactly the puzzle," said Barnacle. "After Sputnik surprised everyone, the United States built a whole new space team called **NASA**, which started its work on **October 1, 1958**. Their very first satellite, called **Explorer 1**, launched on **January 31, 1958** — and it carried that twitchy little needle with it."

Maya pressed her nose near the dial and watched the needle swing wild, then calm, then wild again as the little satellite sailed past.

"It only does it in this one spot," she noticed. "Like there's a ring around the Earth here, even though I can't see it."

Barnacle's whiskers twitched with pride. "You just found it," he said. "Scientists on the ground worked out the very same thing from that very same twitchy needle. There's an invisible belt circling our planet — a wide ring of something that can give a spaceship a little zap, like static electricity jumping off a wool sweater. It's called the **Van Allen belt**, and Explorer 1 is what discovered it."

Maya grinned so wide her cheeks hurt. "I found an invisible thing!"

"You and a satellite," said Barnacle. "Teamwork."

She traced a wide circle in the air with both arms, pretending to hug the whole invisible belt at once. "It's like a hula hoop around the whole world," she said.

"That," said Barnacle, "is the best description of it I have ever heard, and I have heard several."

The little pencil-shaped satellite wobbled past the invisible ring one more time, needle ticking happily, and sailed off toward the dark to keep counting things nobody could see.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Two Trips and One Big Dare (1961)
chapters.text:
Numbers glowed on a square panel floating in the dark: 10... 9... 8...

"A countdown!" Maya shouted, and counted along, loud and fast, right down to one.

With a rumble under her hull, a little round ship zoomed past, spinning gently end over end.

"Who's flying that?" Maya asked.

"A Soviet pilot named **Yuri Gagarin**," said Barnacle. "On **April 12, 1961**, he became the very first human to fly in space, aboard a capsule — that's just a little space car — called **Vostok 1**. He went all the way around Earth once, in about **108 minutes**."

Through a tiny round window, Maya spotted a smiling face and waved both hands. The pilot waved back.

"He's smiling the whole time!" she laughed.

"He smiled his way into history," said Barnacle.

The paper boat drifted sideways, and a second little capsule zipped by, shaped almost the same but painted differently.

"Is that him again?" Maya asked.

"A different flyer," said Barnacle. "An American named **Alan Shepard**. On **May 5, 1961**, he became the first American in space, aboard **Freedom 7**. His trip was shorter and didn't go all the way around, but it still counted as a very big first."

Maya looked from one capsule to the other, back and forth, like watching a race with no finish line yet.

"So who wins?" she asked.

Before Barnacle could answer, a deep, crackly voice came through the little radio — a man giving a big speech.

"Listen," said Barnacle.

"We choose to go to the Moon," the voice said.

Maya's mouth fell open. "The MOON?"

"On **May 25, 1961**," said Barnacle, "President **John F. Kennedy** dared his whole country to land a person on the Moon and bring them safely home, before the decade was done."

Maya grabbed Barnacle's flipper. "Then that's where we're going next. Right?"

Barnacle laughed, a big bubbly sound. "All aboard, Maya. The Moon it is."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Sailing Among the Stars (1963 and 1965)
chapters.text:
A cheerful voice crackled through the radio, humming a little tune between words.

"That's not a man's voice," Maya said, surprised.

"Good catch," said Barnacle. "Can girls go to space too?"

"They sure can," said Barnacle. "Her name is **Valentina Tereshkova**. On **June 16, 1963**, she became the first woman ever to fly in space, orbiting Earth aboard a capsule called **Vostok 6**."

Maya pressed both hands to her chest. "She's a girl, like me."

"Just like you," said Barnacle. "Before she flew, she used to work in a factory. Then she went and circled our whole planet."

Maya watched Tereshkova's tiny capsule loop past, smooth and steady, like a sailboat tacking across calm water. "She sails it so well," Maya whispered.

The paper boat drifted on, and soon a strange sight floated ahead: a person in a puffy white suit, drifting outside a spacecraft entirely, tied to it by a long, thin line.

"Barnacle, he's OUTSIDE the ship!" Maya gasped.

"That's called a **spacewalk**," said Barnacle. "On **March 18, 1965**, a Soviet flyer named **Alexei Leonov** became the first person ever to float outside his ship in open space. He stayed out there about ten minutes."

Maya studied the long line connecting him to his ship. "That rope is like an anchor line," she said. "So he doesn't float away forever."

"Exactly like an anchor line," said Barnacle, clearly delighted. "You'd make a fine ship's captain, Maya."

Maya watched Leonov tumble slowly, arms out wide, turning in lazy circles against the stars, tethered safe the whole time.

"It looks like swimming," she said. "Except there's no water."

"Space swimming," said Barnacle. "I like that. Don't tell the fish."

Maya giggled so hard she nearly rolled off the hull, and had to grab the side of her little paper boat to keep from tumbling right out among the stars herself.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Tallest Thing Maya Ever Saw (1966 to 1968)
chapters.text:
Something blocked out the stars ahead, tall and white and impossibly huge.

Maya craned her neck all the way back. "What IS that?"

"A rocket," said Barnacle. "Called the **Saturn V**. Go on, guess how tall."

Maya squinted at it, trying to picture something she knew that was very, very tall. "Taller than my house?"

"Much taller," said Barnacle.

"Taller than... the Statue of Liberty?" Maya tried.

"Taller than that too," said Barnacle, grinning. "It stood **363 feet** high. The Statue of Liberty would have to stand on her own toes to peek over the top."

Maya let out a low whistle. "Who built something that big?"

"Two men, on two different sides," said Barnacle. "On the Soviet side, a brilliant rocket designer named **Sergei Korolev** led the whole program in total secret. Nobody even knew his name until after he died in **1966**. On the American side, a rocket builder named **Wernher von Braun** led the team that built this very rocket, the Saturn V, for NASA."

"A SECRET rocket builder?" Maya said, eyes huge. "Like a spy?"

"Rather like one," said Barnacle.

The paper boat rose alongside the giant rocket, past its fins, up toward a small capsule perched at the very top. Through its window, three astronauts looked out at a big blue ball hanging in the black sky.

"Is that... Earth?" Maya breathed.

"In **December 1968**, the crew of **Apollo 8** became the first people ever to fly all the way around the Moon," said Barnacle. "One of them, **William Anders**, looked back and took a photo of Earth rising over the Moon's edge. People still call it Earthrise."

Maya grabbed her pencil stub and began sketching fast: a curved gray horizon, a round blue Earth hanging just above it.

"Can I keep this one?" she asked.

"Keep every one," said Barnacle softly. "That's what drawing is for."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Giant Leap (1969)
chapters.text:
Everything went quiet. Even the radio static seemed to hold its breath.

"Why'd it go so quiet?" Maya whispered.

"Watch," said Barnacle.

A spindly-legged ship touched down on gray, dusty ground, soft as a feather landing on a pillow.

Maya counted the rungs of a little ladder leading down its side: one, two, three, four.

A bulky white boot stepped onto the very last rung, then down, down, until it pressed into the dust below.

"That's one small step for man," crackled a voice through the radio, "one giant leap for mankind."

"Barnacle," Maya whispered, "is that the Moon? Really?"

"Really," said Barnacle. "On **July 20, 1969**, astronaut **Neil Armstrong** became the first person ever to walk on the Moon."

A second astronaut hopped down after him, bouncing in slow, bunny-like jumps across the dust.

"That's **Buzz Aldrin**," said Barnacle. "He joined Armstrong down on the surface. A third crewmate, **Michael Collins**, stayed up above the whole time, flying the ship that would carry all three of them home."

Maya watched the lonely ship circling high overhead. "Doesn't he feel left out?" she asked. "Everyone else gets to walk around."

"Maybe a little," said Barnacle. "But somebody has to mind the boat so everyone else has a ride home. That's an important job too."

Maya thought about that, nodding slowly. "Like when I stay by the dock and hold the rope so Mom can tie up the boat."

"Just like that," said Barnacle.

She watched Armstrong and Aldrin bounce across the dust a while longer, planting a flag, picking up gray rocks.

"Did more people get to come after them?" Maya asked.

"Many more," said Barnacle. "Between **1969** and **1972**, twelve astronauts walked on the Moon, across six different trips."

"Twelve!" Maya said. "That's a whole lot of footprints."

"And every single one is still up there," said Barnacle, "because there's no wind on the Moon to blow them away."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Splashdown and a Handshake (1970 and 1975)
chapters.text:
A sharp little ping rang out, and a red light blinked on a far-off capsule.

Maya sat up. "What was that?"

"An oxygen tank had a problem," said Barnacle calmly, steering the paper boat a safe distance away. "This was **Apollo 13**, in **1970**, on its way to the Moon."

"Are they okay?" Maya asked right away.

"They are," said Barnacle. "Smart people down on Earth figured out a fix using only what the astronauts already had onboard. Every single one of that crew made it safely home."

Maya let out a long breath and smiled. "Good. I like stories that end with everybody safe."

"So do I," said Barnacle. "Now — one more stop. The very last one."

The paper boat sailed on, and ahead, two very different spacecraft drifted slowly toward each other: one with American letters painted on its side, one with Soviet ones.

"Are they going to bump?" Maya asked, worried.

"Watch closely," said Barnacle.

The two ships turned, nose to nose, and came together so gently they barely made a sound — parking together in space, like two boats tying up at the very same dock.

"On **July 17, 1975**," said Barnacle, "an American crew and a Soviet crew docked together up there in orbit. The astronauts and cosmonauts opened a hatch between their ships and shook hands."

Maya watched two gloved hands clasp through the open hatch, floating gently in the quiet dark.

"So they stopped racing?" she asked.

"They did," said Barnacle. "That handshake is what ended the whole Space Race — not a winner, but a hello."

Maya smiled, and the paper boat began to glow warm and gold, turning gently for home.

WHOOOOSH, they sailed back through the rainy dark, past the stars, through the round window, and SPLOOSH, settled soft into the little bowl on Maya's nightstand.

Her Earthrise drawing lay tucked safe in her hand. She reached up and taped it carefully to the wall beside her bed, right where she'd see it first thing in the morning.

Barnacle gave one last flipper-wave from the water before slipping beneath the surface.

"All aboard, Maya," he said, "for whatever's next."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. Sleep tight, little sailor — all aboard for dreams of stars.
